This study experiments with solving graph partitioning on the Fujitsu Digital Annealer, a hardware specifically designed for tackling combinatorial optimization problems, and compares its performance to existing top solvers. The results reveal limitations in existing solvers on dense graphs as well as those of the Digital Annealer on sparse graphs, which opens the door to hybridizing these approaches.

In this paper, we identify key properties of finite effect algebras with a state defined. We derive two specific matrices associated with a finite effect algebra E and demonstrate that when E possesses a state, the ranks of these matrices are equal.

Our research into magnetar spectral lines is set against the backdrop of the next generation of high-resolution, high-efficiency X-ray telescopes, which we explore in relation to magnetar activity in its persistent and bursting forms. Building on this foundation, we develop a phase-resolved model for magnetars in a state of dormancy. The outcome of our analysis shows that to fully determine the source and orientation of strong magnetic fields within magnetars, we must simultaneously account for the intensity, breadth and energy of these spectral lines. Furthermore, our computational simulations demonstrate the detection potential of present and future X-ray telescopes in studying magnetar spectral lines and offer promising avenues for exploring both quiescent and bursting emissions within these intense magnetic environments.

This paper investigates the Navier-Stokes equations in the half-plane, under initial conditions that match Euler's model, where a non-zero boundary velocity exists. Assuming the data's analytic properties, we demonstrate the existence of a solution that is unaffected by viscosity, valid for a short, viscosity-independent timeframe. The solution is constructed through an asymptotic expansion, combining the Euler and Prandtl equations' solutions, along with an error term that diminishes in proportion to the square root of viscosity. The Prandtl solution introduces a singular term, which impacts the error's regularity. The error is further decomposed into Euler, Prandtl corrections of the first order, and an additional error. The use of an analytic framework is primarily driven by the nature of the Prandtl equation.

The AFM CrI$_3$ bilayer is a unique representative of van der Waals 2D semiconductors with promising properties in magnetism and spintronics. Using density-functional theory, we have examined the spin texture in momentum space of the highest valence band of the AFM CrI$_3$ bilayer with spin moments aligned perpendicularly to the layers. We found evidence of a Rashba spin texture within the Brillouin zone's central region, arising from the internal electric fields acting on each layer. To study the distribution of wavefunctions between the layers, we applied a small electric field, which caused the degenerate states to separate based on their occupancy. We discovered that the highest valence band wavefunctions are confined to one of the two layers, displaying opposite in-plane spin textures, with segregation occurring across nearly the entire Brillouin zone. This in-plane-canted spin locking is related to the energy gap between the highest AFM band and the other valence bands. Furthermore, we have explained how interactions between the bands can break the layer locking at the $K$, $K'$, and $\Gamma$ points. We also compared the layer locking mechanism in our AFM bilayer system with hidden spin polarization in nonmagnetic centrosymmetric materials, highlighting the differences in segregation mechanisms and their implications for layer locking. We suggest that a similar Rashba effect with in-plane-canted spin locking may occur in other van der Waals AFM bilayers exhibiting strong spin-orbit coupling and an isolated energy band.

Closed-shell pair geminal wavefunctions are directly linked to their scalar products and density matrix elements through their pair amplitudes, mirroring a fermion or boson version of Wick's theorem. The general formula derived from this relationship is complex, but it has been demonstrated how it can be simplified in three different contexts, namely the Richardson-Gaudin model, the antisymmetrized geminal power, and the antisymmetrized product of strongly-orthogonal geminals. Furthermore, dissociation curves for hydrogen chains can be accurately calculated using two alternative approaches based on off-shell Richardson-Gaudin states and the antisymmetrized product of interacting geminals, which suggests that previously obtained incorrect results could be rectified by employing a distinct type of Richardson-Gaudin state.

This research proposes a novel genetic algorithm based resource allocation (GA-RA)
method to optimize energy consumption and maximize throughput in multi-user
massive multiple-input multiple-output (MU-mMIMO) systems that utilize orthogonal
frequency division multiplexing (OFDM) transmission. A hybrid precoding (HP) approach
with three stages is developed: initial RF beamforming, baseband (BB) precoding,
and resource allocation (RA) blocks. First, a single RF beamformer is designed
using the slow time-varying angle-of-departure (AoD) data for all subcarriers to
reduce RF hardware complexity and power consumption. Next, the resulting CSI
is used to create separate BB precoders and RA blocks for each subcarrier. These
are developed using the regularized zero-forcing technique. Finally, the GA-RA
method is used to optimize power and subcarrier allocation for throughput
maximization. Simulation results demonstrate significant throughput enhancements
in MU-mMIMO-OFDM systems via the GA-RA approach compared to traditional equal
RA (EQ-RA) and particle swarm optimization based RA (PSO-RA) methods, particularly
at lower transmission powers and higher numbers of subcarriers.

In this research, we address a key challenge in decentralized systems, where multiple interconnected nodes seek to collaboratively compute the average of their private values without exposing these values to one another. Building on prior work in distributed consensus, we introduce an innovative approach that balances the trade-off between achieving convergence and preserving data privacy. By strategically designing and broadcasting noisy messages, our algorithm allows nodes to converge to the average of local values while minimizing the leakage of sensitive information. This is made possible by carefully measuring the mutual information between private messages and the messages collected by potential adversaries. Our solution is effective across a range of network topologies, ensuring user data remains confidential unless a critical structural vulnerability exists, and provides a flexible trade-off between desired accuracy and the duration of the convergence process.

Recent advancements in multi-agent reinforcement learning rely heavily on training and information exchange methods. However, centralized approaches that eliminate non-stationarity in multi-agent environments come with significant communication overhead. On the other hand, policy sharing in decentralized training is often crucial but lacks theoretical backing. This work identifies a subset of cooperative games where agents' similarities enable policy sharing without compromising performance. Building on this insight, we introduce a decentralized actor-critic algorithm that leverages consensus updates for both actors and critics, ensuring convergence. Furthermore, we develop practical variants of this method to minimize training communication costs without sacrificing policy quality, matching the performance of centralized approaches.

Our research examines the motion of a solid sphere falling through a two-layered fluid under the influence of gravity, assuming an ideal flow scenario. Laboratory experiments at moderate Reynolds numbers of around 20 to 450 show that a sphere with a specific critical density, higher than that of the bottom layer, can exhibit unusual behaviors, such as bouncing or becoming trapped after crossing the fluid interface. We have found that the critical sphere density decreases as the transition layer between the fluids becomes thinner, and increases linearly as the density of the bottom fluid increases, while keeping the density of the top fluid constant. To estimate the critical density, we developed a model based on the sphere's potential energy, which provides an upper limit that is within 5% of the measured critical density values within the density range of approximately 0.997 g/cm^3 to 1.09 g/cm^3.

We have conducted spectroscopic and photometric analyses in UV and optical wavelengths of SN 2020jfo, a Type IIP supernova, which occurred in the spiral galaxy M61. SN 2020jfo displayed a brief plateau period of less than 65 days and reached a maximum brightness in the V-band within approximately eight days of the explosion. Our bolometric light curve estimates suggest the production of 0.033 solar masses of radioactive $^{56}$Ni during the explosion. Spectroscopic data revealed that SN 2020jfo exhibits characteristics typical of Type IIP supernovae, but with a few distinct features, including shallow H$\alpha$ absorption and the presence of $^{58}$Ni at a wavelength of 7378 angstroms in the nebular phase. Through hydrodynamical modelling using MESA + STELLA, we estimated an ejecta mass of approximately five solar masses, suggesting that SN 2020jfo could have originated from a Red Super Giant progenitor with a mass around 12 solar masses at its Zero Age Main Sequence. Modelling of the bolometric light curve revealed the presence of an additional radiation source for the first 20 days, attributed to the interaction with a circumstellar material of approximately 0.2 solar masses, likely ejected due to enhanced mass loss 20 years prior to the supernova explosion.

The electric power system is undergoing significant transformations as a result of the growing reliance on renewable energy sources and the subsequent decommissioning of traditional power plants using synchronous generators. With primary suppliers of ancillary services being gradually phased out, the need for new flexibility and reserve providers is emerging. The increasing prevalence of Distributed Energy Resources (DERs) in modern distribution networks offers opportunities for distribution system operators to fill the market gap by leveraging DER flexibility. This research introduces a novel centralized MPC-based controller, enabling the concurrent provision of voltage support and primary and secondary frequency control through adjustments to the setpoints of a diverse group of DERs in active distribution grids. An input-multirate control framework is employed to account for distinct timescales and provision requirements of each ancillary service, ensuring that available resources are properly allocated. Moreover, a proposed efficient method for incorporating network constraints into the formulation involves applying network decomposition to a linear power flow formulation, combined with network reduction. Additionally, the controller takes into account different timescale dynamics of the employed DERs and their capability curves. The proposed controller's performance is evaluated using dynamic simulations on various case studies, specifically the IEEE 33-bus system.

Percolation encompasses a distinct set of complex problems involving random systems, typically defined by elements placed on a grid or continuous space. Although the setup appears straightforward, many percolative systems exhibit a pivotal transition from isolated clusters to a single, extensive network when a critical threshold is reached. Similar to thermodynamic phase transitions, these systems often exhibit characteristic power-law behaviors near this threshold. Scaling and renormalization theory provides valuable insights into the underlying causes of these phenomena, and these concepts have been effectively utilized to derive quantitative outcomes. In this research, we investigate percolation on a hierarchically structured grid, leveraging a decimation method to obtain precise values for critical exponents. Our calculations yield closed-form solutions for the complete set of geometric critical exponents, which are further validated through simulation results. Furthermore, we establish a novel renormalization framework for the system's conductivity and apply it to extract the conductivity exponent t.

We establish specific instances of Beilinson-Tate conjectures for the automorphic representations of PGSp6 when its Spin L-function has a singularity at s = 1. Utilizing the unique theta correspondence between the split type G2 group and PGSp6, and under the condition that a particular archimedean integral does not vanish, we are able to verify a conjecture put forth by Gross and Savin regarding rank 7 motives of type G2.

We developed an axi-symmetric model of NGC 628 using a radiative transfer code, accounting for the absorption and re-emission of starlight by dust within the galaxy. The model, which includes emission from Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbons and anisotropic scattering, was used to simulate the UV-to-submillimetre images of this nearly face-on spiral galaxy. Our results represent the second successful RT-based modelling of a face-on spiral galaxy and demonstrate that our solution can accurately reproduce the large-scale geometry of stars and dust within the galaxy. Our findings indicate that NGC 628 has not undergone significant inside-out disk growth as predicted by some galaxy formation models. Furthermore, we observed a substantial presence of dust grains at large radii, suggesting the presence of efficient transport mechanisms within the galaxy. Our analysis shows that young stellar populations contribute to 71% of the galaxy's dust emission, while the bulge's old stellar populations contribute to the heating of dust within the central region. Our results also indicate that NGC 628 has a relatively low star formation rate of $\rm SFR=2.00\pm0.15\,{\rm M}_{\odot}{\rm yr}^{-1}$..

Large-scale language models often train on massive datasets but frequently encounter duplicated information, whether by design or due to imperfect data cleansing, exposing the model to identical content at various levels. Research has demonstrated that this repeated data can significantly impede model performance. This paper explores the effects of duplicated data in a systematic manner and delves into its underlying mechanisms. We trained a series of models, with the majority of the data being unique but a small portion being repeated multiple times. Our findings reveal a notable 'double descent' phenomenon, where the model's performance on unseen data deteriorates mid-training due to duplicated information. Interestingly, a specific range of repetition rates leads to substantial declines in model performance, with our experiments showing that even a small percentage of duplicated data (0.1%) can severely degrade a model's capabilities, equivalent to reducing its parameters by half (400M to 800M). We propose that the peak of this degradation lies within a specific range where the model focuses excessively on memorization, potentially consuming a large portion of its capacity. Our research further connects these findings to recent mechanistic interpretability studies by revealing that duplicated data disproportionately compromises the model's ability to generalize, particularly affecting copying mechanisms and induction heads. This provides a possible explanation for why even a small amount of duplicated data in large language models can result in considerable harm to their overall performance.

In this study, we examine the maximin share (MMS) fair allocation of indivisible tasks. Researchers have developed an algorithm for additive valuations, yielding an 11/9-approximate allocation, but it's also known that a better approximation is impossible. However, little is known about MMS allocations beyond additive valuations. We begin by demonstrating that for submodular valuations, the best achievable approximation ratio is n, in contrast to goods where constant approximations have been established. We then focus on two scenarios with combinatorial valuations. In the first, agents must pack items of varying sizes into bins, minimizing the number of bins used. In the second, agents have machines to process items, aiming to minimize processing time. We create constant approximation algorithms for both settings, but show that with a fairness change to proportionality up to one item, the best approximation ratio is still n.

Thin films, measuring less than a micron thick, that form from interstellar material, drift away from the galactic plane due to the force exerted by radiation from nearby stars. These films can develop through the natural accumulation of dust in protoplanetary disks or artificially by the actions of advanced civilizations. Over the course of the Milky Way's existence, they build up and settle above the galactic disk at a specific height, influenced by the mass of dark matter surrounding the galaxy. However, observations of starlight scattered throughout the galaxy suggest that these thin films comprise only a small fraction, approximately 2 times 10 to the power of negative 3, of the overall interstellar medium's mass.

We've developed an algorithm that accurately and consistently identifies the presence of spectral gaps in the energy spectra of quasicrystals, utilizing computational models on finite systems. This algorithm is used to demonstrate the existence of spectral gaps in the Hofstadter model when applied to the Ammann-Beenker tiling, specifically resolving previous inconclusive findings for a particular energy range. Our method is applicable to a broader class of systems with finite local complexity, enabling the identification of all spectral gaps, thus overcoming a previously established limitation on the computational determination of spectral gaps for more general Hamiltonian systems.

Optimizing charging phases for electric vehicles is the central issue we investigate. Our approach involves transforming this challenge into a complex mathematical model that needs to be solved to minimize energy loss during the charging process. To bypass the difficulty of solving this non-linear model, we introduce the PXA algorithm, a relaxation technique that employs matrices representing phase, eXchange, and Adjustment. Our research proves that under specific constraints, PXA consistently finds the global optimal solution. Building upon this algorithm, we also developed PXA-MPC, an online implementation that incorporates predictive control and significantly outperforms traditional empirical phase balancing methods in terms of energy delivery, charging costs, and future energy management. Our results are supported by data collected from an actual adaptive electric vehicle charging network.

We examine the impact of R&D, capital accumulation, and innovation output on the productivity of entrants and incumbent firms in Estonia. First, unlike in developed countries, a small proportion of firms conduct formal R&D, yet a significant percentage of firms still innovate. Second, we found that entrants and incumbents exhibit the same level of R&D elasticity for productivity, but innovation output significantly contributes to productivity, especially among new firms that use an interactive approach to innovation, resulting in productivity gains of 21-30% for entrants and 10-13% for established firms. Third, despite Estonia's typical sectoral composition for developing countries, incumbent firms are able to convert scientific and technological innovations into productivity gains at a comparable rate to developed economies. Fourth, we discovered that the effectiveness of embodied technological change through capital accumulation in fostering productivity growth exceeds that of R&D, but R&D-enhanced firms achieve greater results. Lastly, our findings suggest that productivity-boosting strategies employed in developed economies might not be directly applicable to emerging economies.

Gravitational waves from cold neutron stars yield eigenfrequencies that are complex numbers, with the oscillation frequency represented by the real part and the damping rate by the imaginary part, leading to a two-dimensional eigenvalue problem. However, to simplify calculations, one can adopt an approximation that reduces the parameter space to one dimension. We investigate the validity of the zero-damping approximation, one of the simplest one-dimensional approximations, for fundamental and first-pressure modes of neutron stars, finding it effective for these cases. Nonetheless, the approximation does not apply to the spacetime mode due to its comparable damping rate and oscillation frequency. Nonetheless, we identify an empirical relationship that relates the imaginary and real parts of the eigenfrequency to the star's compactness, regardless of the neutron star matter equations of state. By using this relation, we can express the eigenfrequency solely in terms of the oscillation frequency, transforming the problem into a one-dimensional eigenvalue problem. Consequently, we find that this simplified approximation remains accurate even for the first spacetime mode.

This paper introduces a novel approach called DIST to overcome the limitations of existing knowledge distillation methods. By leveraging a stronger teacher, DIST aims to distill knowledge more effectively. We observe that the discrepancy between the student and teacher predictions can be quite significant. To address this challenge, we propose a correlation-based loss function that preserves the relationships between the teacher and student predictions, capturing the underlying inter-class relations. Additionally, we extend this concept to the intra-class level to account for varying semantic similarities between instances and classes. Our approach is simple yet effective and achieves state-of-the-art performance across image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation tasks, as demonstrated by extensive experiments. The code is publicly available on GitHub.

Building Information Modeling has been utilized for energy efficiency analysis and improvement in buildings, particularly in existing structures where deconstruction and retrofitting are feasible. As cities built without energy-saving knowledge now seek to become more energy-smart, a major challenge lies in scaling BIM generation to larger communities and cities, which is currently a time-consuming and expensive process. In this research, we present an approach for creating prototype buildings, allowing for efficient matching and statistical generation. Our proposed method identifies and upgrades existing buildings with energy-efficient alternatives by leveraging 3D point cloud data. We conduct experiments on a synthetic dataset to validate the efficacy of our approach.

When a single input image is insufficient for object classification, it is essential to leverage complementary information from multiple images depicting the same object from diverse angles to enhance scene understanding and boost performance in the process. However, the task of multi-view image classification is hindered by a major obstacle: data gaps. To address this challenge, we present a novel technique for multi-view image classification that is robust to missing data. Built upon cutting-edge deep learning-based methods and metric learning, our approach is easily adaptable and can be applied to a wide range of applications and domains. Thorough evaluations were conducted on two distinct multi-view aerial-ground datasets, and the results demonstrate that our algorithm significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in multi-view image classification accuracy. The code for our algorithm is available on GitHub at \url{https://github.com/Gabriellm2003/remote_sensing_missing_data}.

This article revisits the concept of smoothing bounds in the context of parallel lattices and codes, initially introduced by Micciancio and Regev, to analyze the security of lattice-based cryptosystems. Without being confined by direct application concerns, we provide a comprehensive study of the techniques used to obtain these bounds for both lattices and codes, and transfer these methods between the two areas. Considering multiple types of spherically symmetric noise distributions, we found that the most effective strategy for achieving the worst-case bound involves a combination of Parseval's Identity, the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, and the second linear programming bound, and this approach is applicable to both codes and lattices and all types of noise distributions. In the case of average-case analysis, we can replace the linear programming bound with a tight average count, which yields optimal results for spherically uniform noise over random codes and lattices. This approach also improves upon the previous Gaussian smoothing bound for worst-case lattices and provides even better results with uniform ball noise, outperforming Gaussian and Bernoulli noise for codes and lattices respectively. However, upon closer examination, we found that by decomposing and truncating Gaussian and Bernoulli distributions into a superposition of uniform noise, we can further improve the results for these cases and bring them on par with the uniform cases.

This research evaluates the potential of well-established quantum computing algorithms for fault-tolerant quantum computing to model the laser-induced electron behavior in small molecules such as lithium hydride, utilizing a quantum computer simulator for computations. The results obtained from these simulations are compared with the time-dependent full configuration interaction method, showing accurate wave packet propagation and time-dependent dipole moment calculations using the Jordan-Wigner transformation, Trotter product formula, and Hadamard test. To incorporate non-Hermitian operators into the dynamics, a similar approach to the quantum imaginary time evolution algorithm was used, allowing for the accurate simulation of ionization in a hydrogen molecule with a complex absorbing potential. Importantly, the quantum algorithms used scale polynomially rather than exponentially, making them suitable for significant advances in understanding the electron dynamics of larger molecular systems in the future.

We investigate how the equivalence principle interacts with an extended uncertainty principle that accounts for the effects of spacetime curvature over large distances. We discover that, when the modified uncertainty relations apply, the weak form of the equivalence principle is compromised, since the inertial mass of quantum systems varies depending on position, whereas gravitational mass remains unaffected. This finding is obtained by analyzing spinor and scalar fields separately, within the context of non-relativistic versions of the Dirac and Klein-Gordon equations, incorporating the extended uncertainty principle. Notably, in both cases, the ratio of inertial to gravitational mass remains constant.

$^{180m}$Ta, an abundant naturally occurring isomer and the longest-lived nuclear isomer discovered, holds significant interest in various fields such as dark matter research, gamma laser development, and astrophysics. Although its excitation energy remains unmeasured directly, its estimated value is derived from a nuclear reaction data analysis. We utilized the high-precision mass spectrometer JYFLTRAP to determine the excitation energy of $^{180m}$Ta with high accuracy, finding a mass difference between its ground and isomeric states to be 76.79(55) keV. This is the first direct measurement of the excitation energy and provides a higher level of accuracy than the previous estimate of 75.3(14) keV.

To investigate the properties of nearby active galactic nuclei, we employed three prominent models linking their radiative efficiency with parameters such as supermassive black hole mass, disk orientation, and total energy output. The results revealed a negative correlation between the spin of these black holes and cosmic time, aligning with theoretical predictions for similar objects. Furthermore, our analysis showed that spin is positively correlated with both black hole mass and total energy output, a finding consistent with theoretical expectations. Notably, a significant proportion of these active galactic nuclei exhibit spin values in the range 0.75-1.0, with approximately 40% possessing spin greater than 0.75 and about 50% possessing spin greater than 0.5. These findings are in line with our previous research and corroborate similar conclusions from other studies.

Our evaluation of the "optimal fingerprinting" methodology as presented by Allen and Tett (1999) is examined through the lens of statistical inference in light of McKitrick's (2021) recent critique.  The review concludes that the "optimal fingerprinting" methodology would withstand the majority of McKitrick's (2021) criticism under two circumstances: (i) the null simulation of the climate model is independent of the actual physical measurements and (ii) the null simulation accurately estimates the residual covariance matrix of the physical measurements, which is contingent on both the calibration and the reliability of the climate models.  If the second condition fails to meet, the estimator will remain unbiased and consistent under typical conditions, but will forfeit the "optimal" advantage of the approach.  The residual consistency test suggested by Allen and Tett (1999) is a valid means for verifying the agreement between the residual covariances of the null simulation and the actual physical measurements.  Additionally, we elucidate the connection between the "optimal fingerprinting" methodology and the Feasible Generalized Least Square.

Historically, sign language resources have been gathered within structured environments for specific projects requiring supervised sign identification or linguistic analysis with predefined annotations. Surprisingly, limited research has focused on extracting information from sign language videos found on social media, combined with the use of unsupervised methods for such resources. The growing demand for models to accurately interpret data differing from training datasets highlights the need for increased diversity in sign language resources, moving away from data collected in controlled laboratory settings. Furthermore, the labor-intensive process of collecting and annotating sign language data suggests the benefits of streamlining this process, which this paper seeks to address by leveraging online data and automated phoneme clustering to create annotated sign language corpora.

Person-tracking robots have a wide range of uses, including security systems, elderly care services, and social robots. However, tracking an individual in a crowded area can be a particularly difficult task. Notwithstanding significant advancements in tracking technology reported in research, state-of-the-art trackers have largely neglected to address the challenge of person following in such crowded scenarios. In this study, we concentrate on enhancing a robot's perception for a person following task by developing a reliable and real-time applicable object tracker. We introduce a new robot person tracking system, called Deep Tracking with RGB-D (DTRD), which is robust against the challenging aspects of uniform crowd environments. Our tracker employs a transformer-based encoder-decoder architecture that combines RGB and depth information to distinguish the target person from similar distractors. Extensive experiments and results confirm that our tracker outperforms other state-of-the-art trackers in terms of performance.

We examine the thermoelectric properties of two-dimensional materials that exhibit two Dirac bands and a nonlinear band, employing a three- or two-band model and the linearized Boltzmann transport theory with the relaxation time approximation. The three-band model demonstrates that pairing Dirac bands with a heavy nonlinear band, regardless of its parabolic or pudding-mold shape, yields comparable thermoelectric performance. The primary distinction between the models is the position of the nonlinear band relative to the Dirac bands, which influences the maximum figure of merit (ZT). For the three-band model with a nonlinear band, optimal ZT values occur when the nonlinear band intersects the Dirac bands near the Fermi level. Conversely, by omitting the linear conduction band and transitioning to the two-band model, we observe superior thermoelectric performance, characterized by higher ZT values.

Mobile devices with advanced computing capabilities, combined with stationary anchors installed indoors, provide a common solution to meet the growing need for indoor location-based services. Among the existing indoor localization methods, those utilizing Bluetooth Low Energy anchors, Received Signal Strength, and lateration are widely adopted due to their cost-effectiveness and widespread device accessibility. However, BLE- and RSS-based systems often suffer from inaccuracies caused by signal fluctuations, insufficient anchor placement, device hardware variability, and anchor distribution issues. This paper addresses these challenges by implementing a collaborative indoor positioning technique that leverages nearby devices as supplementary anchors in an expanded network. A multilayer perceptron neural network is applied to analyze the collaborating devices' information, including estimated positions and BLE-RSS data, taking into account device specificity to determine relative distances. Following this, lateration is applied to derive collaborative device positioning estimates, which are then combined with standalone estimates to provide a final device position. Experimental results confirm that the proposed collaborative approach surpasses the standalone lateration method in terms of positioning accuracy.

This research focuses on analyzing polarized gravitational waves that emerged from chiral fermions in the early universe's formative stages. Specifically, we concentrate on the contribution of left-handed neutrinos in thermal equilibrium, with a finite temperature and chemical potential, during the universe's radiation-dominated era. We calculate the correlation functions of gravitational fields related to the Stokes parameter V, which indicates the circular polarization of gravitational waves in both Minkowski and expanding spacetime settings. In an expanding universe, we observe that thermalized neutrinos produce a non-zero V value directly proportional to the neutrino degeneracy parameter and the wavenumber of gravitational waves in the long-wavelength region. Although the intensity of gravitational waves generated by thermal neutrinos is too weak to be detected by current or planned third-generation gravitational wave detectors, future generation detectors for high-frequency ranges could potentially reveal information about the neutrino degeneracy parameter in the early universe.

Research on empirical distribution functions (EDFs) based on ranked set sampling (RSS) and its modifications has been widely explored by numerous authors, primarily focusing on infinite population settings. In contrast, developing EDF estimators for finite populations is more beneficial in fields like environmental science, ecology, agriculture, and biology. This study proposes novel EDF estimators based on level-0, level-1, and level-2 sampling designs within RSS and examines their asymptotic properties. Numerical results demonstrate the superiority of level-2 sampling design in achieving a more efficient EDF estimator, especially under imperfect ranking conditions. Furthermore, the application of RSS based on level-2 sampling design is showcased through a real-data analysis of estimating a distribution function and the median weight of seven-month-old sheep.

Our investigation focuses on how a binary companion influences black hole superradiance, particularly when their orbital frequencies are not in the gravitational-collider-physics (GCP) resonance range. When the tidal disturbance from the companion causes a superradiant state to couple with an extremely absorbent state, the superradiance rate becomes suppressed. However, as the binary separation decreases below a specific threshold, the superradiance rate turns negative, and the surrounding boson cloud is ultimately absorbed by the black hole. This binary separation boundary imposes tight constraints on GCP, especially for companions with a mass ratio exceeding $10^{-3}$, which effectively cancels out nearly all GCP and Bohr transitions apart from those involving the $|\psi_{211}\rangle$ state. Furthermore, the gravitational backreaction on the companion manifests as a torque exerted on the binary, producing unstable orbits detectable through pulsar timing. Notably, the potential termination of cloud growth may help to relax the current mass constraints of ultralight bosons imposed by several non-observations.

A clear indication of Beyond Standard Model physics is charged lepton flavor violation. 
This overview covers both theoretical and experimental findings related to charged lepton flavor violation in heavy particle decays, specifically focusing on the Z and Higgs bosons, and top quark. 
We also examine the potential for charged lepton flavor violation in hypothetical particle decays such as those from a Z' or additional scalar particles. 
Lastly, we assess the potential for such searches at upcoming high-energy electron-positron colliders.

The phase $\phi_s$ from CP violating interactions, $B_s$ decay widths and their differences, are crucial indicators of potential new physics and limitations in heavy quark expansion theories. Future research on $Z$ factories suggests significant measurement possibilities. By optimizing the operating conditions, researchers can achieve precision: $\sigma(\phi_s) = 4.3~\mathrm{mrad}$, $\sigma(\Delta\Gamma_s) = 0.24~\mathrm{ns^{-1}}$ and $\sigma(\Gamma_s) = 0.072~\mathrm{ns^{-1}}$. The $\phi_s$ precision at $Z$ factories is comparable to that of the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider (HL-LHC) LHCb resolution, requiring 30% less precision. At 10-Tera-$Z$ mode, $\phi_s$ precision can reach 41% of the HL-LHC LHCb resolution, and 10-Tera-$Z$ mode enhances $B_s$ decay widths and their differences by 18%.

Recent findings have led researchers to investigate how different anatomical brain structures, specifically gyri and sulci, contribute to various functions. To better understand this complex relationship, a universal theory and efficient computational model are needed, but the highly non-linear and highly variable nature of brain function has hindered progress so far. To address this, our team has developed a novel model that leverages brain function gradients derived from resting-state fMRI to predict individual cortical folding patterns. By combining a mesh convolution model with an attention block, our model effectively accounts for spatial variations and interprets functional gradients' contributions. Experimental results demonstrate that our model outperforms existing state-of-the-art models and offers valuable insights into the relationship between brain function and anatomy. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the primary functional gradients have less impact on folding prediction and that well-known brain landmarks are often situated at the periphery of highly active regions rather than within them. These results suggest that custom-designed artificial neural networks can enhance the accuracy of mapping brain functions to cortical patterns, shedding new light on the intricate anatomy-function connection in neuroscience.

We propose the integration of Terahertz and Gigahertz electromagnetic waves in a cryogenic environment where electrons float on a liquid helium surface. Terahertz waves are nearly synchronized with the frequency of electron transitions between the surface state's lowest energy levels, while Gigahertz waves induce a Stark effect, causing symmetry-breaking among electrons on helium. Our research demonstrates a cooperative effect between these two types of electromagnetic waves, which occurs at the threshold where the detuning between electrons and Terahertz waves matches the frequency of Gigahertz waves. By combining their influences, the Terahertz and Gigahertz waves collaborate to stimulate electrons, producing low-frequency electrical currents perpendicular to the helium surface. These currents can be measured using the image-charge method, providing an alternative approach for Terahertz detection.

Static code warnings generated automatically are plagued by a high incidence
of false alarms, causing developers to disregard the majority of them. To
enhance the effectiveness of these warnings, analysts should refine their
algorithms to identify optimal parameters for tackling their specific issue.
By doing so, they can develop predictive models that adjust the decision
threshold to better distinguish actionable from inconsequential warnings. Our
study demonstrates that such methods can significantly improve the detection of
actionable static code warnings. In our experiments on eight Java projects, we
obtained perfect accuracy on 50% of the datasets and a median AUC score of
92% across all datasets.

We examine the condition of essential self-adjointness for the drift-diffusion operator $H=-\frac{1}{\rho}\nabla\cdot \rho \mathbb D\nabla +V$, specifically on domains $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ with $\mathcal{C}^2$ boundary and a broad spectrum of coefficients $\rho,\; \mathbb{D}$, and $V$. By providing criteria, we illustrate how the coefficients' behavior near the domain boundary ensures the essential self-adjointness of $H$. As part of this, we establish a weak, anisotropic Hardy inequality of independent significance.

In this research, we explore the elliptical steady states in the restricted $4$-body problem, where the three dominant masses are aligned in an Euler configuration, and all four bodies exist in a two-dimensional space. We derive the symplectic reduction for this scenario, which is applicable to a broader range of the restricted $N$-body problem. Through an analysis of the connection between this specific problem and Lagrangian solutions, we determine the linear stability of the $4$-body problem using the $\omega$-Maslov index. Additionally, numerical calculations allow us to identify the mass parameters that influence stability in symmetric configurations.

We develop a Rademacher-type theorem involving Hamiltonians $H(x,p)$ under minimal requirements in both Euclidean and Carnot-Carathéodory settings. Specifically, $H(x,p)$ is assumed to be merely measurable in $x$ and quasiconvex and lower-semicontinuous in $p$. The lower-semicontinuity assumption in $p$ is optimal. Furthermore, using this theorem, we establish the existence of absolute minimizers for associated $L^\infty$-functionals, thus advancing or augmenting existing literature results.

Over the past few years, the ability to generate photorealistic images has experienced significant advancements due to breakthroughs in deep convolutional neural networks and generative models. Specifically, face photos have garnered substantial attention, with numerous models being developed to generate and manipulate them. The process of modifying facial attributes involves adjusting the values of one or more attributes without altering the rest of the image. These changes can be specified through an attribute vector or a guiding face image, which are then processed by the corresponding models. This paper reviews recent research in semantic facial attribute editing, covering essential concepts, architectures, evaluation metrics, and applications. The state-of-the-art models are categorized into encoder-decoder, image-to-image, and photo-guided models based on their architectures, and their limitations and challenges are also explored.

Skin cancer's most aggressive form, melanoma, requires a lengthy diagnostic process due to its similarity in appearance to benign lesions. Current diagnosis methods, involving histological examination, are time-consuming and invasive. Developing a precise classifier can significantly improve early detection and treatment of skin cancer, thereby increasing patient survival rates. This study presents a multi-class classification task using CoAtNet, a novel architecture combining the strengths of traditional CNNs and Transformer models. The proposed classifier demonstrates high performance, achieving precision, recall, and AP scores of 0.901, 0.895, and 0.923, respectively, outperforming other advanced networks.

Objective: We aim to refine the orbital characteristics and physical properties, and determine the orbital tilt angle in relation to the sky for five planetary systems with eccentric transits: HAT-P-15, HAT-P-17, HAT-P-21, HAT-P-26, and HAT-P-29. These systems consist of a hot Jupiter, except for HAT-P-26, which hosts a Neptune-class planet. Methods: By observing transit events using the HARPS-N spectrograph, we obtained precise measurements of radial velocities that enabled us to measure the Rossiter-McLaughlin effect in each system. Using new and archived data, including those from Gaia, we further characterized the atmospheric properties of the stars. The photometric parameters of four hot Jupiters were recalculated using new transit data obtained from medium-class telescopes and the TESS space telescope. Data from the HATNet project were also examined for signs of stellar rotation periods and spin axis inclination. Results: Our analysis of the Rossiter-McLaughlin effect led to the determination of the orbital tilt angle in relation to the sky for HAT-P-15b, HAT-P-17b, HAT-P-21b, and HAT-P-29b, with values of 13, -26.3, -0.7, and -26 degrees, respectively. Unfortunately, due to data quality issues, we could not accurately constrain the orbital tilt angle for HAT-P-26b, although a prograde orbit is the most plausible explanation. The stellar activity of HAT-P-21 indicates a rotation period of 15.88 days, allowing us to calculate its true misalignment angle, which is 25 degrees. Our analysis of the physical properties of the five exoplanetary systems returned values that match the existing literature. Using TESS and available transit data, we reviewed the orbital ephemeris of the five systems and confirmed that HAT-P-26 exhibits transit timing variations, which may be attributed to the presence of a third body.

Our investigation into the high-cadence microlensing surveys has led to the
discovery of four new planetary systems. These systems, including OGLE-2017-BLG-1691L,
KMT-2021-BLG-0320L, KMT-2021-BLG-1303L, and KMT-2021-BLG-1554L, feature planets with
mass ratios as low as 10^-4. The planets were detected despite short observation
periods, ranging from a few hours to several days, thanks to the combined data from
the microlensing surveys. The discovered planets have sub-Jovian masses, with three
of them corresponding to roughly 0.10, 0.38, and 0.12 times the mass of Jupiter. The
mass of the remaining planet, located in the system OGLE-2017-BLG-1691L, is similar
to that of Uranus. The mass of the host star in the system KMT-2021-BLG-1554L is at
the boundary between a star and a brown dwarf, approximately 0.08 times the mass of
the Sun. The other planetary host stars are relatively low-mass, ranging from 0.3 to
0.6 solar masses. These discoveries highlight the capability of current high-cadence
microlensing surveys to detect low-mass planets.

In scientific computing, a wide array of applications necessitates the approximation of mappings between Banach spaces. Recently introduced methods, such as the Fourier Neural Operator and the Deep Operator Network, can fulfill this requirement. However, their approach of sampling input functions on a grid and parameterizing output functions with neural networks results in 1) unintelligible output and 2) systematic bias caused by aliasing errors. We propose an alternative in this article, suggesting the use of Chebyshev and Fourier series for both the input and output domains. This yields the Spectral Neural Operator, characterized by transparent output, immunity to aliasing, and the capacity for many exact function operations. The underlying functionality relies on established, fast, and stable spectral methods, requiring only standard numerical linear algebra. Our comparative studies demonstrate that the Spectral Neural Operator outperforms both the Fourier Neural Operator and the Deep Operator Network for many operators.

Currently, state-of-the-art natural language understanding models, like Transformers, have a tendency to produce unreliable predictions or wildly inaccurate probability scores. This makes it challenging to make informed decisions based on their output. We introduce the inductive Venn-ABERS predictors (IVAP), a type of predictor that ensures well-calibrated predictions under minimal assumptions, utilizing pre-trained Transformers. We assess their performance across various NLU tasks and demonstrate that they generate reliable probability scores evenly distributed between 0 and 1, while maintaining the original model's level of accuracy.

A $k$-dimensional $[n,k]$ binary linear code, denoted as $\mathcal{C}$, can be viewed as a subspace of $\mathbb{F}_2^n$. For any vector $\boldsymbol{x}$ in $\mathbb{F}_2^n$, the set $\boldsymbol{x}+\mathcal{C}$ constitutes a coset of $\mathcal{C}$. Our research focuses on a partial ordering among the cosets of a given binary linear code of length $n$, with an emphasis on graph construction based on its orphan structure.

We introduce a straightforward and effective approach to named entity linking (NEL)
utilizing entity representation through multiple embeddings. To validate the effectiveness
and evaluate the parameter sensitivity of our method, we assess its performance on Namesakes,
a notoriously challenging dataset characterized by ambiguous entity names. Our analysis reveals
that the minimum number of mentions necessary to establish a knowledge base entity is a crucial
factor influencing NEL performance, whereas the number of embeddings is relatively unimportant
and can be minimized with as few as ten or fewer. Additionally, we demonstrate that our entity
representations can be refined solely using knowledge base data, resulting in improved NEL performance.
We also compare the NEL performance of embeddings derived from fine-tuning a language model on a
diverse set of news articles to embeddings obtained by fine-tuning on a more homogeneous dataset
comprising public sources like XSum, CNN/Daily Mail. Notably, fine-tuning on diverse news articles yields
better embeddings.

In MARL, our alternative approach involves a learned facilitator that aggregates
and interprets information from agents, enhancing their overall performance without
becoming a central controller. This is achieved by encouraging agents to be less
reliant on the facilitator's messages and by limiting its influence to policy
selection rather than immediate action, thereby allowing agents to maintain control.

This investigation scrutinizes the underlying security assumptions of three prominent public-key quantum money schemes. In 2012, Aaronson and Christiano developed a system leveraging hidden subspaces within the space $\mathbb{F}_2^n$, while in 2015, Pena et al speculated that the core problem could be resolved in quasi-polynomial time. To confirm this hypothesis, a new polynomial-time quantum algorithm was designed to solve the underlying challenge, relying on calculating the Zariski tangent space of a random point within the hidden subspace. Meanwhile, Zhandry's scheme based on multivariate hash functions from 2017 has been found vulnerable due to a newly developed polynomial-time quantum algorithm capable of producing counterfeit banknotes with high probability, utilizing the verification circuit. Additionally, Kane, Sharif, and Silverberg's 2021 quaternion algebra scheme was targeted with a new polynomial-time quantum reduction that transforms its hard problem into a simpler linear algebra problem, potentially paving the way for further analysis and critique.

We establish necessary and sufficient conditions for Gorenstein-projective modules over certain types of rings, extending existing results by relaxing the compatibility requirements of the underlying bimodules. This work builds upon previous findings for specific types of algebras and provides a broader generalisation. We also demonstrate an application of our results in a noncommutative context, specifically for Noetherian rings and modules.

Measurements of differential cross sections for Compton scattering from protons have been conducted at various angles using polarized gamma-ray beams with a central energy of 81.3-83.4 MeV, carried out at a research facility called the Triangle Universities Nuclear Laboratory. The results were compared to previous findings and analyzed through chiral effective field theory to determine the proton's electromagnetic properties, specifically its dipole polarizabilities, yielding a value of 13.8 $\pm$ 1.3 for electric polarizability and a negligible value for magnetic polarizability in units of 10$^{-4}$\, fm$^3$.

This document focuses on efficiently implementing large-scale constant multiplication using a single variable within a shift-adds framework, minimizing the need for adders and subtractors. Given the complexity of this issue, an approximate algorithm, referred to as T~OLL, is introduced, which segments large constants into smaller ones. To minimize operation counts, T~OLL incorporates graph-based and common subexpression elimination methods that were previously proposed for shift-adds designs. Additionally, this approach considers the delay of multiplierless designs by taking into account the maximum number of operations in series, i.e., adder-steps. Experimental findings show that applying T~OLL leads to significant reductions in adder-steps at a relatively low cost in the number of operations. Notably, gate-level results reveal that the shift-adds design achieves a 36.6% reduction in area compared to a design using a multiplier. Furthermore, delay-aware optimization can result in a 48.3% decrease in the minimum achievable delay of the shift-adds design when compared to area-aware optimization.

Recent advancements in large language models, such as Codex, have demonstrated their potential to produce code for a wide range of programming tasks. However, existing models often struggle with complex tasks due to a fundamental flaw: they lack a deep understanding of program semantics. Consequently, their output frequently contains errors that prevent compilation. In this research, we investigate the efficacy of automated program repair (APR) techniques in rectifying the mistakes generated by these models, specifically in the context of LeetCode contests. Our objective is to determine whether APR can boost the reliability of code produced by large language models. The findings of our study indicate that: (1) code generated automatically shares common programming errors with manually crafted solutions, implying that APR may be effective in fixing auto-generated code; (2) by leveraging statistical fault localization techniques to pinpoint the location of bugs, the newly introduced Codex edit mode performs comparably to or exceeds the capabilities of existing Java repair tools, such as TBar and Recoder. Our analysis of these experimental results yields several key suggestions: (1) enhancing APR tools to overcome limitations in their search space, such as improving fault localization, is desirable; (2) as large language models continue to learn from additional data, future APR tools could focus on more advanced, synthesis/semantics-based approaches, rather than merely accumulating more fix patterns; (3) exploring the integration of language models with APR to create more refined patch ingredients is an area worthy of investigation.

In this context, we're examining a deviation from Einstein's theory of gravity within a specific setup involving the Neumann boundary condition. This boundary condition represents an end-of-the-world brane within the framework of the AdS/BCFT correspondence in AdSd+1 spacetime, where d is greater than 2. We derived an explicit mode expansion of the perturbations for the case of a tensionless brane. Furthermore, we've found that the energy-momentum tensor of a d-dimensional boundary conformal field theory (BCFT) must adhere to certain constraints in addition to those associated with boundary conformal symmetry when interacting with a specific gravity condition. This condition can take the form of the Neumann or conformally Dirichlet boundary conditions. Notably, we've verified that these constraints are satisfied for a free scalar BCFT. It was also discovered that in the context of the AdS/BCFT correspondence, a tensionless brane allows a BCFT to couple with a gravity having the Neumann boundary condition. On the other hand, for a nonzero tension brane, the BCFT can couple with a gravity having the conformally Dirichlet boundary condition by leveraging holographic relations.

This paper investigates ways to enhance the masked image modeling (MIM) technique by introducing key modifications.
MIM allows the model to identify key image features by masking the input image and having the unmasked sections predict the missing parts. We have identified three areas where MIM can be improved.
First, despite encoders and decoders contributing to representation learning, MIM solely employs encoders for downstream tasks, thus disregarding the influence of decoders. We argue that continuing to minimize decoder parameters will enhance the encoder's representational capabilities. Second, MIM resolves the image prediction challenge by simultaneously training encoders and decoders, rather than designing a distinct task for the encoder. To boost the encoder's performance for downstream tasks, we implemented tasks for comparative learning and token position prediction specifically for the encoder. Third, as the input image may consist of backgrounds, additional objects, and varying proportions of each object, reconstructing tokens related to backgrounds or other objects holds little significance for understanding main object representations. Consequently, we employ ContrastiveCrop to crop the input image to contain the main objects as much as possible. Based on the proposed enhancements to MIM, we introduce a new model called Contrastive Masked AutoEncoders (CMAE). Our proposed model yielded a Top-1 accuracy of 65.84% on the tinyimagenet dataset, utilizing the ViT-B backbone. This outcome outperforms competing methods by +2.89 when conditions are equal, and the source code will be released.

Pre-trained language models, particularly ones like BERT, are highly effective for large-scale text retrieval tasks. Current text retrieval systems with exceptional performance typically follow a two-stage approach due to the computational expense associated with pre-trained models and the size of their corpora. In the past, researchers primarily focused on optimizing individual components of these frameworks to enhance overall retrieval performance. However, there is a gap in understanding how to integrate features from multiple stages of these frameworks for optimal performance. This study addresses this limitation by proposing Hybrid List Aware Transformer Reranking (HLATR), a subsequent reranking module that combines retrieval and reranking features. HLATR's lightweight design allows it to seamlessly integrate with existing retrieval systems, facilitating efficient processing of reranking tasks. Experimental results on large-scale text datasets demonstrate that HLATR significantly enhances the ranking performance of existing multi-stage text retrieval methods.

Recent advancements have led to the development of mean-field equations to approximate opinion formation in the Deffuant model. These equations effectively describe both fully-mixed populations and populations interacting through network edges. Interactions in this context occur only between individuals with differing opinions within a specific threshold, known as the confidence bound. This parameter's magnitude has a significant influence on the model's dynamics and the formation of opinion clusters. This work aims to conduct a mathematical analysis of the mean-field equations to examine the role of confidence bounds and their boundaries on key model observables. We explore the scenario where the confidence interval is narrow, and reveal the underlying mechanisms driving opinion evolution. Our results show that linear stability analysis can predict the formation and location of opinion clusters, and numerical simulations demonstrate that the model's early-time dynamics and final cluster locations can be accurately approximated for various network configurations, including those with two degree classes and fully-mixed populations.

We present DeepFlame, an open-source C++ platform that integrates machine
learning capabilities and pre-trained models to solve reactive flow problems by
utilizing the strengths of OpenFOAM, Torch, and Cantera. DeepFlame simplifies
inter-library communication to facilitate code maintenance, modification, and
upgrades. Our platform is demonstrated by applying deep learning techniques for
predicting chemical kinetics to accelerate reacting flow simulations. Through a
range of canonical cases, we validate the accuracy and efficiency of the
convection-diffusion-reaction algorithms implemented in DeepFlame. The results
reveal robust performance in both steady-state and transient simulations. Moreover,
we explore methods to enhance computational efficiency, including dynamic load
balancing and adaptive mesh refinement. Our tests on a medium-end GPU and a deep
computing unit (DCU) show that DeepFlame achieves significant speed-up of two
orders of magnitude, particularly for hydrogen ignition, and holds promise for
further gains with hydrocarbon fuels and next-generation computing hardware.

A light source at distance d will have its signal reach detectors spaced 100 AU apart at differing times of up to 120(d/100 Mpc)^{-1} nanoseconds due to wavefront curvature. With gigahertz interferometry, arrival time differences as small as a nanosecond can be detected. Given positional accuracy of detectors to a few centimeters, achieved through interferometry or GNSS geolocations, nanosecond timing enables precise cosmological measurements, rivaling those of other long-distance measurement techniques. A constellation of four detectors, placed at distances greater than 10 AU from the Sun, would allow for precise distance calculations of light sources with an error margin of less than 1%, thus permitting accurate measurements of the Hubble constant. The precision of distance calculations increases in proportion to the square of the baseline length. Fast radio bursts (FRBs) are the brightest known point-like extragalactic radio sources, and their precision can be limited by Galactic scattering at frequencies below 3 GHz, and by dispersion effects at higher frequencies. On the other hand, with baselines longer than 100 AU, time delays caused by Shapiro effects become a limiting factor but can be corrected by incorporating additional detectors. Furthermore, positional inaccuracies of detectors caused by various astrophysical effects could be corrected through periodic trilaterations using a setup like GNSS. Alternatively, combining precise accelerometer measurements with calibration based on distant FRBs might provide an effective solution. In addition to cosmological applications, the proposed interferometer would also resolve the radio emission of Galactic pulsars, determine the mass distribution in the outer Solar System, and detect gravitational waves at frequencies ranging from 0.01 to 100 micro-Hz.

Investigations into the physical and chemical properties of line-emitting gas systems rely heavily on plasma diagnostics. It is crucial to accurately correct the input spectrum for extinction to perform plasma diagnostics effectively, as the determination of extinction degree is closely tied to the physical properties of the line-emitting gas. Consequently, both extinction correction and plasma diagnostics must be conducted simultaneously and consistently. Our study of nine bright planetary nebulae in M 31, comparing analyses performed with and without proper extinction correction and plasma diagnostics, illustrates the detrimental impact of making incorrect initial assumptions about the physical conditions of the line-emitting gas in extinction correction. Although electron density and temperature are relatively unaffected by these assumptions, compromised extinction leads to systematic errors in line strengths, which in turn compromises the derived ionic and elemental abundances and other inferences. The sample of M 31 planetary nebulae represents the high-mass end of the mass range for low-mass planetary nebula progenitor stars, consistent with existing theoretical models. Our findings suggest that previous claims of anomalously high nitrogen abundance in these PNe were likely caused by underestimating extinction due to inconsistent assumptions in extinction correction. The validity of previous plasma diagnostics results must be reassessed with simultaneous self-consistency with extinction correction.

We define a sequence of polynomial measures known as $q,t$-Catalan measures, which reside in $\mathbb{R}^2$. These measures are determined by area, dinv, and bounce properties on continuous paths and exhibit numerous combinatorial similarities to $q,t$-Catalan numbers. Our key finding shows that $q,t$-Catalan measures are the limiting form of a sequence of $q,t$-Catalan numbers, denoted $C^{(m)}_n(q,t)$, as the value of $m$ approaches infinity. Furthermore, the $q,t$-Catalan measures are interpreted geometrically as the Duistermaat-Heckman measures of punctual Hilbert schemes that parameterize schemes of $\mathbb{C}^2$ centered at the origin.

To address the issue of disconnected reasoning in QA, where models rely on shortcuts rather than multi-hop reasoning, a novel approach is proposed. The method, called counterfactual multihop QA, leverages a causal-effect approach to reduce disconnected reasoning. It involves modeling the causality of disconnected reasoning and true multi-hop reasoning, then using a counterfactual inference to disentangle these effects and promote the use of multi-hop reasoning in QA models. Experiments on the HotpotQA dataset demonstrate the method's efficacy in reducing disconnected reasoning, with notable improvements in performance achieved through the use of true multi-hop reasoning.

CORL is an open-source library offering one-file implementations of Deep Offline Reinforcement Learning algorithms. It prioritizes a hassle-free development process by utilizing a clean and straightforward codebase along with a contemporary metrics tracking tool. In CORL, individual methods are separated into distinct files to simplify performance-related aspects recognition. Furthermore, CORL provides a cloud-based logging system for tracking experiment metrics, hyperparameters, and dependencies. Lastly, to guarantee implementation reliability, CORL has benchmarked its code against the D4RL standard. CORL's source code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/tinkoff-ai/CORL.

In recent times, transformer-based models have achieved notable success in semantic segmentation, but traditional CNN-based methods continue to lead in real-time applications due to the transformer's computationally intensive nature. To bridge this performance-efficiency gap, we propose the RTFormer, a high-efficiency dual-resolution transformer designed for real-time semantic segmentation, which outperforms its CNN-based counterparts in terms of both performance and efficiency. The RTFormer utilizes a GPU-friendly attention mechanism with linear complexity and eliminates the need for the multi-head mechanism to ensure fast processing on GPU-like devices. Furthermore, we've found that utilizing cross-resolution attention allows for more efficient collection of global context information for the high-resolution branch by spreading knowledge learned from the low-resolution branch. Our extensive experiments on well-established benchmarks have demonstrated the RTFormer's superiority, achieving state-of-the-art results on Cityscapes, CamVid, and COCOStuff, and promising results on ADE20K. The implementation details can be found in the PaddleSeg repository on GitHub.

As self-supervised models continue to grow in size, compressing them has become increasingly important. However, reducing model size is not the only effective method for decreasing computational costs, as shortening input sequences can also yield significant improvements. This study examines fixed and variable-length sampling methods along the time axis within self-supervised learning to determine their impact on specific downstream tasks. Our results show that sampling while training these models not only enhances performance on these tasks at optimal frame rates, but it also significantly accelerates inference. Notably, variable-length sampling outperforms others under low frame rates, and with access to phonetic boundaries, performance degradation can be entirely avoided even at very low average frame rates, such as 10 Hz.

We demonstrate that the multiplicative Grothendieck-Springer space inherently possesses a quasi-Poisson structure. The corresponding group-valued moment map arises as the resolution morphism, while the quasi-Hamiltonian leaves correspond to the connected components of the preimages of Steinberg fibers. This finding is a multiplicative counterpart to the standard Poisson structure on the additive Grothendieck-Springer resolution, serving as an explicit example of a broader reduction method along Dirac realizations, which has been explored in recent research by the author and Mayrand.

We present a quantum field theory model that describes spin-half particles in curved spacetime, grounded in the principles of general relativity and covariance. This framework enables the calculation of various observables for particles in a gravitational field, including spin precession even without torsion. Notably, this effect contrasts with the free-fall non-universality we previously observed for massless particles. Furthermore, the quantum-particle energy related to the gravitational potential remains unaffected by wave-packet dispersion in Earth's gravitational field, which underlies the non-universality of free fall in quantum mechanics. This theoretical finding opens an additional experimental route for testing our model via gravitational spectrometry. Finally, the model reveals that fermions and antifermions cannot be distinguished in gravitational interactions.

Determining the complex patterns within multivariate data sets is a central challenge in statistics and artificial intelligence. Conventional methods focus on the underlying probability distribution, but their effectiveness is often hindered by the exponential growth of data dimensions. Conversely, modern machine learning approaches typically rely on black-box models, which lack the guarantee of providing reliable insights. In this study, we concentrate on developing a more efficient and transparent method for learning multivariate cumulative distribution functions. By leveraging their inherent properties, such as handling of mixed variables, efficient calculation of probability intervals, and the ability to mitigate data scarcity, we propose an innovative approach to overcome the limitations of existing methods. We demonstrate that a low-dimensional representation of a multivariate cumulative distribution function can be obtained by decomposing it into a naive Bayes model using a tensor-rank decomposition. By introducing a low-rank model, either directly or indirectly through data transformation, our approach enables efficient sampling, exact inference, and uncertainty estimation while ensuring uniqueness of the model under relatively mild conditions. We showcase the superior performance of our proposed model on various synthetic and real-world datasets and applications, including regression analysis, data sampling, and imputation. Notably, our experiments indicate that it is possible to achieve better density estimates indirectly through a low-rank cumulative distribution function model, rather than a low-rank probability distribution function model.

In the context of autonomous navigation, where remote sensors have limited power and bandwidth, we explore the use of event-triggered estimation to reduce communication expenses. To achieve this, we have developed an efficient sampling-based planner, which generates motion plans and corresponding communication strategies. These strategies minimize costs while ensuring that the system meets the necessary safety and success criteria. Furthermore, we have developed an offline method to calculate the expected distribution of the system's state, and we have derived bounds on this distribution. These bounds enable us to evaluate the system's safety constraints, which are then used in our algorithm. Through case studies, we have demonstrated the effectiveness of our approach in computing optimal navigation plans efficiently.

Observational evidence suggests a hard energy spectrum for specific types of ultrahigh energy cosmic rays when they reach Earth, indicating their composition is dominated by heavier elements. However, such hard spectra can be explained if just a few sources are responsible for the majority of ultrahigh energy cosmic rays at the highest energies. If these sources are located at great distances, time delays from interactions with the extragalactic magnetic field could filter out lower-energy cosmic rays, resulting in a steeper energy spectrum observed at Earth. By focusing on radio galaxies as a primary source of ultrahigh energy cosmic rays, conditions are established under which a limited number of active sources would surpass the collective contributions from many other sources that have been active in the past. Two scenarios are presented, demonstrating that a source's lifetime must be comparable to the expression ${t_{\rm act} \sim \left( B/1\,\text{nG} \right)^2\,\left( d_{\rm src}/10\,\text{Mpc} \right)^2\,\left( l_{\rm coh}/1\,\text{Mpc}
\right)\,\text{Myr}}$ to achieve the required hardening of the cosmic ray spectrum at Earth, assuming specific properties for the extragalactic magnetic field.

Although instance-level GNN explanation techniques are well-established, the task of explaining the overall behavior of a GNN remains under-explored and holds significant value for interpretability and troubleshooting. Current methods either provide a list of local explanations for a specific class or generate a hypothetical, high-scoring graph, neglecting the combinatorial aspects of the GNN's learned knowledge. This work introduces GLGExplainer, the first global GNN explanation model that can create explanations as complex Boolean expressions of the learned graph concepts. By combining local explanations into a logical formula over graph clusters, GLGExplainer generates accurate and interpretable global explanations that align with ground-truth or existing domain knowledge. The extracted formulas closely match the model's predictions, enabling GLGExplainer to serve as a valuable diagnostic tool for evaluating GNNs and identifying incorrect model rules.

State-of-the-art solutions often incorporate encoder-decoder architectures as key components, which are commonly used in various fields that rely heavily on deep learning models. Despite growing efforts to develop interpretation tools for these models and integrate symbolic representations with deep learning in the neuro-symbolic community, there is still a pressing need for better visualization tools for understanding the inner workings of deep learning architectures. Encoder-decoder models present a unique opportunity for humans to visualize and edit the knowledge encoded in model weights, and our work focuses on creating an abstraction that enables segments of the network to be represented as a two-way graph-based system. This approach allows for changes in the graph structure to directly impact the underlying tensor representations, paving the way for novel neuro-symbolic systems that combine the strengths of pattern recognition and symbolic reasoning. As a result, our approach is expected to not only facilitate new ways of interacting with deep learning models but also enhance their overall performance by harnessing the power of learning and reasoning capabilities.

This research introduces an efficient method for determining the hidden components of Bayesian state space models. The proposed algorithm, a variant of simulated-based inference methods that utilize multiple artificially generated datasets, involves training a versatile model to forecast the relevant variables. In contrast to previous approaches, the method described here enables the development of hidden state estimators by focusing solely on specific aspects of marginal posterior distributions and incorporating prior knowledge. The algorithm's efficacy is demonstrated through the analysis of stochastic volatility models, nonlinear dynamic stochastic equilibrium models, and seasonal adjustment models with changing seasonality. Notably, following a several-hour initial training phase, the model can calculate posterior distributions for any dataset in just a fraction of a second.

Recent advancements in self-supervised learning from speech data have yielded models that excel in various tasks and capture underlying speech signal characteristics. Despite their capabilities, the performance of these models on prosody-related tasks remains largely unexplored. We introduce an evaluation framework, SUPERB-prosody, which assesses 15 self-supervised speech models on three prosody tasks and two related subtasks. Our results demonstrate that 13 of these models outperformed the baseline in all prosody tasks, and also show promising performance on two additional tasks: prosody prediction and forecasting. We further dissect the contribution of each layer in these models and conclude that self-supervised speech models are highly adept at addressing prosody-related tasks.

Our research begins by attempting to develop an automated system for detecting bias in Bing and Google search results, utilizing cutting-edge techniques. Additionally, we investigate gender bias in YouTube search results, focusing on how the narrator's gender is perceived by viewers. Although our top-performing model's class-wise accuracy is not sufficient for automated bias analysis, we instead employ manual annotations to assess perceived gender bias in YouTube search results.

This presentation reviews the automated next-to-leading order (NLO) corrections for
Standard Model processes in both hadron and lepton collider simulations within
WHIZARD. Emphasis is placed on NLO electroweak and QCD-electroweak interference corrections
at the LHC. Recent advancements regarding electroweak corrections for future lepton
