To set these prices, a complex optimization problem was formulated to balance peak demand reduction and benefits for both consumers and utility companies. This problem was then simplified to make it easier to solve and evaluated for its effectiveness using various case studies that demonstrated significant peak demand reduction and economic benefits for all parties involved. Additionally, simulations showed that the simplified solution method did not sacrifice any of the original problem's potential solutions, further validating its practicality.

Geschke demonstrated the existence of a 3-saturated, clopen graph in the space $2^\omega$, whereas clopen graphs in the same space cannot have even a 4-saturated infinite subgraph, though a specific $F_\sigma$ graph is known to be $\omega_1$-saturated. Interestingly, there is no closed graph in $2^\omega$ that achieves $\omega$-saturation. In this paper, we complement existing findings by showing that for every $n$, there is an $n$-saturated, closed graph in the Cantor space $2^\omega$. This conclusion relies on a probabilistic lemma, whose main construction involves the inverse limit of finite graphs.

A subset of a permutation group's elements is considered intersecting if any two elements within it share a common image under the group's action. For a transitive permutation group, the maximum intersection density is determined by the size of intersecting subsets relative to the stabilizer of a point. A group with a stabilizer of maximum intersecting size is said to possess the Erdős-Ko-Rado property, which this study examines for permutation groups with point stabilizers of prime order, particularly focusing on orders 2 and 3 which lack this property. Additionally, the paper presents infinite families of permutation groups with point stabilizer of order 3 and varying intersection densities.

We determine equilibrium radiation levels and decay times resulting from synchrotron radiation for interconnected storage ring designs by projecting established radiation integral calculations onto the lattice's coupled motion modes, accounting for orbit distortion through off-axis radiation integral assessments. Moreover, we derive concise formulae facilitating efficient forward calculation, which have been integrated into the interactive lattice design software, OPA.

The galaxy CSS J102913+404220 exhibits a distinctive and powerful optical outburst, which we have extensively studied through a decade of multi-wavelength photometric and spectroscopic observations. Our data reveal that mid-infrared flares, which reached an unprecedented peak luminosity exceeding log(L_4.6um)>44 erg/s, occurred approximately two months following the optical outburst, exceeding the luminosity of the most explosive supernovae by a factor of ten. This unusual light curve pattern suggests that the optical outburst might be caused by a stellar tidal disruption event (TDE). Furthermore, we have discovered that the galaxy's X-ray emission brightened by a factor of 30 after 100 days and then faded by a factor of 4 within two weeks, displaying extreme variability. Notably, this variability pattern was accompanied by a stable UV and MIR continuum but an increase in the H-alpha emission line by a factor of about a decade after the nuclear outburst, which has never been observed in other Active Galactic Nuclei (AGNs). This anomaly can be attributed to the replenishment and excitation of gas clouds within the Broad Line Region (BLR) by the interaction of stellar debris with the BLR, as predicted by recent simulations.

The phenomenon of picture-word interference occurs when visual processing is influenced by language processing, with certain words embedded in images affecting how humans perceive them. This language bias has also been observed in artificial models like OpenAI CLIP, which is trained on joint texts and images. By investigating whether this language bias leads to similar interference as seen in humans, researchers can gain insight into how well these models have learned semantic representations from combined language and vision training. To assess this, researchers used methods from cognitive science to develop a benchmark task that tests whether superimposed words on images can distort image classification across various category levels and determine if this distortion is due to shared language and vision semantic representations. The results of this task, applied to the CLIP model, showed that presenting words does affect image classification, but this effect is independent of the semantic relationship between images and embedded words. This suggests that the CLIP model's word representation has a strong influence on visual processing, but does not directly share semantic meaning with image representations.

To combat pandemics like COVID-19, essential resources like personal protection equipment (PPE) are crucial to minimize transmission rates and safeguard individuals close to infected patients. As outbreaks escalate, local production facilities are overwhelmed by skyrocketing demand for these items (Heymann and Shindo, 2020; Klompas et al., 2021). Disruptions in global supply chains caused by factory shutdowns and transportation limitations exacerbate resource scarcity (Ranney et al., 2020, Wu et al., 2020). Initially, the pandemic sparked a reflex of prioritizing local needs (Baldwin and Evenett, 2020). However, our research reveals that implementing a cooperative sharing system significantly enhances the ability to manage epidemics. By establishing a network where communities can pool resources and redistribute them as needed, local resource depletion can be prevented and overall infection rates decreased. Moreover, the effectiveness of resource sharing is contingent upon sufficient time lapsing between outbreaks in separate communities, which necessitates global measures to slow the spread of infections. Our study serves as a starting point for designing a more resilient global supply chain that can proactively address future pandemics, rather than merely responding to chance distributions of resources and opportunities.

To address the significant cold-start issue in click-through rate prediction, we present the Variational Embedding Learning Framework (VELF), a universal framework that resolves data-scarcity induced overfitting in two approaches: by acquiring probabilistic embeddings, and by leveraging trainable and regularized prior knowledge from the rich supplementary information of cold-start users and advertisements. These two techniques are organically incorporated into a variational inference model, enabling an end-to-end training process. Our framework's efficacy is clearly demonstrated by extensive testing on standard datasets, and further experiments confirm that our adaptable and regularized prior models surpass traditional fixed prior models in terms of generalization capability.

A major obstacle in current and future neutrino research using large Liquid Argon detectors is distinguishing between actual neutrino interactions and overwhelming cosmic-ray background. While conventional filtering methods can be effective, they require computationally intensive reconstruction algorithms beforehand. In contrast, our work showcases an innovative approach employing a 3D submanifold sparse convolutional network that leverages raw data from LAr-TPC scintillation light signals to detect neutrinos. By applying this technique to ICARUS simulations, we achieved a remarkable 76.3% reduction in cosmic background with a neutrino interaction selection efficiency of over 98.9%. Furthermore, to address potential inaccuracies in simulated data, we integrated domain-adversarial neural networks that artificially mimic real-world data. Our experiments successfully demonstrated the efficacy of this approach in minimizing biases and yielding superior neutrino interaction detection rates.

Researchers have lately shown significant interest in constructing LDPC codes using permutation matrices. However, a key consideration when working with these codes is preventing the occurrence of short cycles in the corresponding Tanner graph, which typically involves maximizing the code's girth. This paper offers a systematic approach for developing constructions of such codes. By connecting criteria for cycle existence to certain numerical concepts, specifically those associated with Sidon sets, we are able to derive examples of LDPC codes that satisfy specific girth requirements. Furthermore, our framework is expanded to also enable the creation of irregular LDPC codes.

We categorize singularities at infinity of cubic polynomials in three variables,  $f(x_0, x_1, x_2) = f_1(x_0, x_1, x_2) + f_2(x_0, x_1, x_2) + f_3(x_0, x_1, x_2)$,  where $f_i$ are homogeneous polynomials of degree $i$, with $i = 1, 2, 3$. Using this classification, we calculate the Milnor number jump for isolated singularities at infinity, as we transition from a special fiber to a generic fiber. Furthermore, we use these results to investigate global fibrations of cubic polynomials in $\mathbb{C}^3$ and explore the topology of fibers within each equivalence class.

We've developed a variant of the standard Bayesian mechanism, which considers player outcomes and constraints before they're implemented. This model accurately represents a common form of modern online advertising where advertisers prioritize their expected utility over time and their type may change. We're investigating the incentive compatibility issue within this Bayesian mechanism, under the assumption that the conditions for the mechanism environments are relatively weak. We've found a full characterization of incentive compatibility through the taxation principle and discovered that these compatible mechanisms are all essentially variations of auto-bidding, which are widely used in the online advertising industry.

Araci et al. introduced a $p$-adic distribution based on the Haar model, extending its properties. This $p$-adic distribution was used to develop a Volkenborn integral. The author of this paper leverages the Mahler expansion of continuous functions to establish a derivative theorem in relation to the $p$-adic distribution on $\Bbb Z_p$.

A complex network of decision-making agents is considered, guided by a quantum decision-making theory where utility, attractiveness, and information interact. This interplay results in a multi-modal decision-making process. Agents exchange information, either directly received from peers or collectively generated, influencing a shared information field. This common field tends to mitigate sharp probability fluctuations and, in cases of short-term memory, can even lead to oscillating probability values that persist indefinitely, symbolizing perpetual indecision. However, introducing the shared information field dampens these oscillations, causing the probabilities to converge to stable values, thereby describing a phenomenon known as the dynamic disjunction effect.

M. Bhargava and P. Harron demonstrated that for $n=3,4,5$, the arrangements of integers within the rings of $S_n$-number fields of degree $n$ become evenly spread out when the fields are ordered based on discriminant. Building on this, we map the number fields to grids that retain more information from the number fields, where the space of these grids is a layered structure over the space of these arrangements. We expand on Bhargava-Harron's finding by proving that the arrangements of integers within the rings of $S_n$-number fields are evenly spread out across the grid space.

Conversational Search (SCAI) has established itself as a prominent platform that highlights recent innovations in conversational search technology. Last year, SCAI'21 held its first online event and organized a conversational question answering shared task. Notably, all participating teams employed answer generation models for this task. Consequently, evaluating answer accuracy became a significant hurdle and a current knowledge gap in this area. To supplement automatic evaluation, we carried out two crowdsourcing experiments to gather annotations for the plausibility and faithfulness of provided answers. Following the shared task, the original conversational QA dataset used for assessment was enriched with alternative correct answers generated by the participating systems.

We have developed a specific implementation of the adaptively compressed exchange operator within the linear augmented plane wave method. The adaptively compressed exchange operator allows for a low-rank representation of the Fock exchange, thereby maintaining precision in the total energy calculations. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated in a study involving non-relativistic calculations using a hybrid exchange-correlation functional, PBE0. The resulting data show a high level of accuracy for light atoms and molecules, with results deviating from precise calculations by a few microhartree. The combination of this method and the use of high-energy local orbitals were crucial in achieving such a high level of precision in the calculations. We utilize this implementation to calculate PBE0 gaps in solids and compare the obtained results with other all-electron calculations.

A notable active galactic nucleus (AGN), NGC 1566, displays recurrent X-ray outbursts, each lasting several years. In 2018, the AGN underwent a significant X-ray outburst, increasing its flux in the 2-10 keV band by a factor of approximately 24. We re-examined data from the XMM-Newton and NuSTAR space telescopes for three time periods: before, during, and after the outburst. We confirmed the presence of a broad emission line in the 5-7 keV band during the outburst, which is likely due to relativistic iron K-alpha radiation. Our findings indicate that the flux of this emission line increased in tandem with the X-ray continuum, much like a previous instance in another AGN, NGC 2992. This suggests that X-rays originate from a corona above the accretion disk and that the disk reflection produces the relativistic iron K-alpha line. Furthermore, we observed a rapid response (in just four months) of the narrow iron K-alpha emission line to changes in the X-ray continuum, allowing us to infer the location of the line-emitting region as less than 0.1 parsecs. We found that the rate at which the iron K-alpha line varies is higher in NGC 1566 than in NGC 2992, possibly due to the presence of more gas or a higher iron abundance in the former. We also discovered a correlation between the strength of the variable broad iron K-alpha line and the soft X-ray excess emission, which is consistent with the idea that the changing-look phenomenon is associated with a state transition triggered by changes in the accretion rate.

In this study, a social learning model is analyzed where agents randomly select a neighbor's information at each time step. The model reveals that even with reduced communication, agents ultimately acquire accurate information, and the long-term rate of convergence is comparable to traditional methods that require more communication. Furthermore, a specific scenario where an agent replaces its belief with the chosen neighbor's belief is analyzed to provide large deviation estimates of the log-belief ratios.

More than two decades ago, Abadi et al. developed the Dependency Core Calculus
as a fundamental framework for analyzing dependencies within typed programming languages. 
This dependency analysis has led to various significant advantages for language design, 
including the ability to enforce security protocols, identify and eliminate redundant code, 
and other applications. Building upon this concept, our work introduces the Dependent Dependency Calculus 
(DDC), which adapts this idea to dependently-typed languages. By leveraging this calculus, 
we can efficiently monitor the irrelevance of code at both runtime and compile time, 
ultimately leading to faster type-checking and program execution.

The ability to compensate for nonlocal dispersion between broadband photon pairs propagated over ITU-T G.652D telecommunications fiber was studied through precise measurements of their temporal correlation. By adjusting the distance the photons traveled, near-optimal levels of dispersion compensation were achieved, preserving timing correlations within the detection device's resolution limit (41.0$\pm$0.1ps). Experimental results show that such high levels of compensation are feasible with substantial fiber lengths (1km), making it suitable for real-world applications. Furthermore, timing correlations were maintained down to 51ps$\pm$21ps over two separate, 10km segments of deployed metropolitan fiber.

Online food review platforms heavily rely on accurate reviews and personalized
recommendations. Nevertheless, evaluating food and providing suggestions can be
challenging due to diverse contexts and interpretations. This study employs
various deep learning techniques to tackle sentiment analysis, automated review
categorization, and review retrieval for the food industry. At Nanyang Technological
University (NTU), we created the NTU Food Hunter - an internet-based food review
system, integrating deep learning strategies that facilitate users' food choices.
Initially, we integrated the BERT and LSTM deep learning models for analyzing
food reviews. Subsequently, a POS algorithm was developed to automatically identify
and extract adjective-noun pairs from the review content for generating tags
based on POS tagging and dependency parsing. Furthermore, a RankNet model was
employed for re-ranking retrieval outcomes to enhance the precision of the Solr-based
food reviews search system. The experimental outcomes confirm the potential of
our proposed deep learning approaches in solving real-world problems.

We examine the sensitivity of various spin states, including spin-squeezed and Dicke states, that have been split into multiple modes, making them accessible and manipulable in experiments. We derive mathematical formulas that describe how these states enhance the precision of multiparameter measurements and identify the best approaches for achieving the highest sensitivity. Additionally, we investigate the entanglement of these states by developing a test to detect genuine entanglement among $k$ components. Our findings demonstrate the benefits of entanglement for distributed sensing applications and propose optimal methods for estimating multiple parameters using nonclassical spin ensembles that have been spread across space.

Our research involves studying the melting and undercooling processes in tiny (100 nm in radius) gold particles suspended in a vacuum chamber using a highly sensitive trap. These particles are heated using a laser and their temperature and evaporation rate are determined through two primary methods: by measuring the particle's mass and by analyzing the light reflected off its surface. By repeatedly heating and cooling the particles and varying their size, we can investigate how the melting behavior is affected. We also induce undercooling, a phenomenon where the gold remains in a liquid state below its melting point, and compare our findings to theoretical predictions using carefully designed laser pulses.

We undertook the task of translating Emile Mathieu's paper, titled 'On the five-fold transitive function of 24 quantities,' into English to facilitate our research project focused on expressing $M_{23}$ in terms of additive functions on a finite field with 2048 elements.

Our research focus is on network alignment (NA), the process of determining the node correlations between two networks based on both their structure and node attributes. Most current NA approaches attempt to identify all node pairs simultaneously, thus failing to utilize information gained from intermediate node matching to improve the accuracy of subsequent correlations. To address this limitation, we introduce Grad-Align, a novel NA method that identifies node pairs progressively, leveraging the strong correlations found in the early stages of the matching process. To achieve this, Grad-Align first generates node embeddings for the two networks using graph neural networks along with a unique loss function that incorporates neighborhood structures of varying orders. Next, node alignment is performed by calculating dual-perspective similarity metrics, including a multi-layer embedding similarity and Tversky similarity, which can handle networks of different scales. To further enhance structural consistency, Grad-Align incorporates an edge augmentation module. Our extensive experiments with real-world and synthetic datasets demonstrate that Grad-Align consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art NA methods.

In populations, disparities in wealth or resource distribution are notable
features that warrant study. Understanding the underlying causes and effective
strategies for mitigating these disparities is crucial. To investigate this
issue, we propose a model that simulates interactions among agents within a
network aimed at diminishing capital distribution inequalities. By framing the
outcome of elementary games in the network, where winning translates to reduced
inequality, we explore various interpretations of this framework and their
influence on agent behavior in terms of capital distribution. Our analysis
draws on the capital-dependent Parrondo's paradox, offering examples and
insights into the dynamics of inequality formation in society.

Recurrent-based recommender systems have effectively modeled the evolution of user preferences over time. Nevertheless, recurrent neural networks struggle with capturing long-term trends. As a result, recommendation systems that rely on RNNs often focus on users' immediate preferences at the expense of long-term needs. This phenomenon is known as the recency bias, which has the potential to negatively impact user satisfaction and the overall system health. In this study, a novel method called recency dropout is proposed to mitigate the recency bias in recurrent-based recommendation systems. The efficacy of recency dropout is demonstrated through experiments conducted in a simulated environment, offline tests, and real-world trials on a large-scale commercial recommendation platform.

Minimum flow decomposition is a fundamental problem in computer science with applications in RNA assembly in bioinformatics. Despite its NP-hard nature, most practical tools use heuristics or simplified, polynomial-time solvable versions, potentially resulting in suboptimal or incomplete solutions. Traditional integer linear programming (ILP) approaches have limitations due to their requirement to encode a vast number of solution paths. Currently, the only exact MFD solver is inefficient and cannot be easily generalized to real-world scenarios. Our research presents the first efficient ILP formulation for MFD, enabling fast and exact solutions for even the most complex instances. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on both simulated and real-world data sets, with most instances being solved within 13 seconds. Our ILP formulation also offers flexibility and can be easily adapted to accommodate various real-world constraints, such as paired-end reads or flow error minimization. Our results have the potential to overcome the trade-off between complexity and tractability in multi-assembly models, enabling more effective RNA assembly tools.

The issue of determining a smooth cosmic distance ladder from a single location in a non-uniform universe is addressed. The method of anchoring distances to Type Ia supernovae relies on nearby local measurements. We explore how this method works in a perturbed universe with small fluctuations on a flat spacetime. Our findings indicate that a notable 11% modification to the background spacetime distance is caused by inhomogeneities near the observer. This modification is linked to tidal deformations in the local spacetime and is represented by the electric part of the Weyl tensor. The impact of this modification on Type Ia supernova absolute magnitude calibration is examined in detail, potentially resolving the tensions in supernova magnitude and Hubble constant measurements without requiring dark energy.

This research examines a hypothetical universe scenario where phantom energy is dominant and the cosmological equation of state parameter $w$ is less than $-1$. The analysis focuses on the far-future's asymptotic behavior and whether a universe-ending Big Rip singularity could be imminent. Within the framework of general relativity, it's suggested that a gravitational process could potentially prevent the Big Rip, assuming no additional mechanisms create new particles. In this theoretical model, the far-future universe is described as having a high and constant Hubble rate and energy density, accompanied by low and constant horizon entropy, mirroring conditions present at the universe's inception. This analysis indicates that the Big Rip might be averted and the universe may evolve into a new, inflationary phase, ultimately giving rise to the creation of multiple new universes.

Inertial navigation systems rely heavily on gyroscopes to detect rotation. Efforts to improve gyroscope precision beyond classical limitations using quantum resources have gained significant attention. Current quantum gyroscope designs are hindered by decoherence, as stated by the no-go theorem in noisy metrology. A new approach, employing two quantized optical fields as quantum probes, has been proposed, which circumvents the constraints imposed by the no-go theorem. Our detailed analysis of non-Markovian noise reveals that optimal sensitivity at the super-Heisenberg limit can be restored if each optical field forms a bound state with its surroundings. This outcome offers practical guidance for achieving precise rotation sensing in noisy real-world environments.

A new type of Boltzmann-Gibbs random field is proposed, where the energy functional of local field states is defined by an exponential expression. This model incorporates interactions between local states using a spatial coupling function based on smoothed kernel approximations, inspired by smoothed particle hydrodynamics. A second-degree polynomial interaction is explored, resulting in an explicit, mesh-free expression for the spatial coupling function when using a squared exponential smoothing kernel. This allows the model to transition smoothly from discrete to continuous field representations, and connections to Gaussian Markov random fields and Matérn fields are established.

We revisit the concept of itinerant ferromagnetism in 2D and 3D electron systems, taking into account significant spin-orbit effects and strong electron-electron interactions. We've isolated key scattering events occurring near the Fermi surface, which contribute to the destabilization of ferromagnetic quantum critical points at low temperatures. Unlike previous theoretical research, our study demonstrates that these critical processes cannot be entirely eliminated, even with arbitrary spin-orbit splitting present. Our self-contained and non-perturbative analysis of electron-electron interactions near the phase transition confirms that these resonant processes inevitably destabilize ferromagnetic quantum critical points, resulting in a first-order phase transition. Notably, the characteristics of these processes can be observed through the non-analytic behavior of the spin susceptibility in response to magnetic fields, whether at a distance from or close to the phase transition.

In a multi-source system where each source generates updates following a Poisson distribution and is served according to a variable service time, we've introduced a preemptive policy that prioritizes fresh updates from the same source and derived its effect on the average and peak age of information. We've also analyzed two alternative policies: a source-agnostic preemptive policy and a non-preemptive policy, and used the results to evaluate their performance in a two-source system. Our findings suggest that the optimal policy depends on the service time distribution, and that higher moments of the age of information are crucial in determining the best policy.

Gaussian processes serve as a fundamental tool in modeling continuous data in machine learning and statistics. When a process's value is known at a finite set of points, one can use Gaussian processes to create an interpolating surface for predicting and quantifying uncertainty at other locations. However, not all data is presented in this manner; instances like boundary value problems feature information on a domain's boundary, which comprises an uncountable number of points intractable to Gaussian process techniques. To address this issue, we develop a Gaussian process model leveraging reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces, which bridges the gap between finite and uncountable data collections. By establishing the equivalence of conditional expectation and orthogonal projections, we provide a framework for handling such data in statistical models, including its numerical implementation and a proof of concept.

Deep learning-based liver and lesion segmentation has gained significant attention in medical practice due to the rising liver cancer incidence. Although several advanced networks have been developed for medical image segmentation, they face difficulties in accurately identifying liver lesions. To address this challenge, a novel approach combining convolutional and transformer-based architectures has been proposed. The resulting hybrid network, called SWTR-Unet, consists of a pre-trained ResNet, transformer blocks, and a common Unet-style decoder path. The SWTR-Unet was tested on clinical liver MRI scans and publicly available CT data from the LiTS challenge, and its performance was compared to state-of-the-art networks. Additionally, a correlation analysis and ablation study were conducted to identify key factors influencing segmentation accuracy. The SWTR-Unet outperformed other networks, achieving high Dice similarity scores for liver and lesion segmentation on both MRI and CT datasets. The method's performance is comparable to expert manually performed segmentations, and it has the potential to significantly reduce clinical time and resource consumption.

Recent research has revealed that deep neural networks can be compromised by
adversarial attacks, specifically 3D attacks on point clouds. Although prior
methods have generated adversarial point clouds, they exhibit limited transferability
and are easily defendable. In response, this paper introduces a novel point cloud
attack called AOF, which focuses on the low-frequency aspect of point clouds to
create more effective adversarial samples by combining losses from both the
point cloud and its low-frequency component. Experiment results demonstrate that
AOF significantly enhances transferability compared to current state-of-the-art
attacks, and proves more resilient against leading 3D defense techniques. Moreover,
AOF-generated adversarial point clouds feature increased deformation over outliers.

The effects of nuclear structure on the number of produced particles (N_ch) and anisotropic particle movement ($v_2$ and $v_3$) in the isobaric collisions of Ru + Ru and Zr + Zr at different energies (7.7, 27, 62.4 and 200 GeV) are examined using the string melting version of the AMPT model. Comparing the results with recent STAR collaboration data, it is found that nuclear shape influences particle movement, with quadrupole deformation affecting central collisions, octupole deformation impacting near-central collisions, and neutron skin effects dominating mid-central collisions, with these effects being more pronounced at lower energies.

The IWVI theory is revisited, a method for training latent variable models, which employs novel variational bounds called Monte Carlo objectives, obtained by replacing intractable integrals with Monte Carlo estimates derived from importance sampling. A 2016 study established that increasing the number of importance samples results in tighter bounds between the likelihood and the estimate. This insight is used as the foundation for nonasymptotic results exploring the relationship between Monte Carlo estimates and the tightness of these objectives. Contrary to expectations, research suggests that smaller Monte Carlo variance may not necessarily result in better bounds, while negative correlation can actually reduce the variational gap. These findings, which align with empirical evidence from previous studies, also generalize the original monotonicity theorem to accommodate non-uniform weights. This work leverages concepts and results from stochastic orders theory to discuss the practical implications of these theoretical results.

We investigated the behavior of a continuous agent population in a two-resource congestion game where agents follow an Experience-Weighted Attraction algorithm. The system is governed by three key parameters: population rationality (a), memory loss (sigma), and resource asymmetry (b). Our research reveals that altering these parameters leads to various bifurcations, transitioning the system from stable convergence to complex dynamics, including limit cycles and chaotic behavior. We demonstrated that increasing the population rationality (a) destabilizes the system, regardless of the memory loss factor (sigma). Interestingly, as the memory loss factor (sigma) increases, chaotic regimes give way to periodic orbits, indicating that forgetting past outcomes can simplify the system's dynamics and improve predictability. This complexity was further illustrated through simulations and bifurcation diagrams, which showcase the intricate population dynamics, even in simple games.

Neural networks known as capsule networks have achieved notable success in computer vision tasks. Despite this, original capsule networks struggle to reach optimal performance on complex datasets due to their high computational and memory demands. To overcome these limitations, we propose a novel network architecture, called Momentum Capsule Network, which is influenced by reversible Momentum ResNets. These reversible networks make it possible to recalculate forward pass activations during backpropagation, leading to significantly reduced memory needs. In this research, we present a framework that demonstrates how invertible residual building blocks can be integrated into capsule networks. Furthermore, our experiments show that Momentum Capsule Networks outperform traditional capsule networks on MNIST, SVHN, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100, all while requiring substantially less memory. The accompanying source code is available on https://github.com/moejoe95/MoCapsNet.

To rigorously discuss continuous functions, a fundamental concept in mathematics, 
we must first establish a clear definition of open sets in a given space, which 
is achieved by defining a topology through a set of axioms that govern their 
behavior. The modification of one of these axioms in a topology and its impact 
on function continuity is the primary focus of this research.

Solving the problem of finding the shortest paths in connected graphs can be challenging, especially when edge costs need to be modified dynamically in response to specific requirements. However, it's possible to represent pathfinding problems using neural networks by converting cost values into synaptic weights. This enables online adaptation of the network weights using learning mechanisms, which results in solutions identical to those obtained from the Bellman-Ford algorithm. Notably, the proposed neural network has the same computational complexity as the Bellman-Ford algorithm. Furthermore, the network's learning mechanisms can be used to adapt the weights, thereby augmenting the paths according to specific tasks. This is demonstrated through applications such as navigating around obstacles and following specific node sequences in an environment. As a result, the presented novel algorithm opens up new possibilities for applications where path augmentation is directly linked to pathfinding in a natural way.

The existence of the axion particle remains uncertain, but its field can be leveraged in a specific formulation of a U(1) gauge theory with both classical and quantum invariance. Analogues of the axion field, recently developed, can be used in a comparable construction of non-Abelian gauge theories, taking into account their unique symmetries. In this approach, the gauge symmetry is broken, resulting in the gauge boson acquiring mass by incorporating axion particles, which are consequently not considered fundamental particles in this context.

We investigate four-dimensional N=1 gauge theories with S-confining properties, which are equivalent to Wess-Zumino models. Classification of S-confining theories with simple gauge groups already exists, so we instead focus on proving the listed S-confining dualities under the condition that matter fields transform according to rank-1 and/or rank-2 representations. We make minimal assumptions based on established S-confining dualities for SU(N) with N+1 flavors and Usp(2N) with 2N+4 fundamentals. Our strategy involves a series of deconfinements and re-confinements, carefully tracking the superpotential at each step.

We investigate the local and bipartite entanglement R\'enyi entropies of a free Fermi gas within thermal equilibrium in a multi-dimensional space of Euclidean type $\mathbb{R}^d$. We demonstrate that entanglement entropies, defined by the R\'enyi index $\gamma\leq1$, remain positive across all temperatures above zero. Furthermore, for any non-negative R\'enyi index, we identify the asymptotic properties of these entropies when the temperature and a scaling parameter are extremely large, within two different regimes characterized by either a fixed chemical potential or a fixed particle density. This work completes the missing piece needed for a comprehensive proof of our previously established low and high-temperature findings, which were initially presented for $\gamma=1$ in J. Phys. A: Math. Theor.

In photonic quantum information, the discrete Fourier transform (DFT) is a crucial element, however, it's challenging to apply to high-dimensional systems due to limitations in physical encoding methods. A new study demonstrates that high-dimensional frequency-bin DFTs can be efficiently achieved using a three-component quantum frequency processor by introducing additional radio-frequency harmonics. Numerical simulations confirm the effectiveness of this approach with high gate fidelity and success probability. Additionally, the method was experimentally tested and utilized to measure entanglement and perform full tomography in three-dimensional systems. These findings open up possibilities for high-dimensional frequency-bin protocols in quantum communication and networking.

This research builds upon our prior work examining spherical representations within operator algebra. Firstly, we develop potential equivalents to dimension groups in the current context, using operator systems as a foundation. Subsequently, our findings are applied to the inductive limits of compact quantum groups, and we establish a parallel concept to Olshanski's notion of spherical unitary representations for infinite-dimensional Gelfand pairs of the form G < G × G. This, notably, vindicates Ryosuke Sato's methodology in asymptotic representation theory for quantum groups.

The solution of the Klein-Gordon equation for a scalar field in a Kerr black hole environment, initially proposed by Detweiler, is often employed in studying black hole stability and axion-like particles. This research verifies a previously noted discrepancy in Detweiler's solution, which was first highlighted by Pani, and corrects the equation with a missing factor of one-half. The corrected result, however, reveals some unusual properties that question the conventional power-counting strategy. To address this issue, we introduce the next-to-leading order (NLO) correction and find it effectively halves the percentage error of the initial solution for all crucial $r_g \mu$ values. Furthermore, the NLO solution maintains a compact form, rendering it straightforwardly applicable.

In the realm of natural language understanding, natural language inference is a key task that requires determining the connection between pairs of sentences. Current contrastive learning approaches, which utilize relationships from natural language inference datasets to learn sentence representations, have limitations in only focusing on sentence-level comparisons. This paper proposes Pair-level Supervised Contrastive Learning (PairSCL), a novel method that utilizes a cross attention module to learn joint representations of sentence pairs. A designed contrastive objective pulls together similar sentence pairs and pushes apart dissimilar ones. When evaluated on public natural language inference datasets, PairSCL achieved an average accuracy improvement of 2.1% over other methods and also surpassed the previous state-of-the-art on seven text classification transfer tasks.

A notable research project dubbed the "isobar run" at RHIC aimed to investigate the effects of nuclear charge on collision outcomes, specifically by comparing Zr and Ru isotopes. However, recent STAR data revealed more pronounced differences between these isotopes than initially anticipated. Multiple studies have sought to quantify their shape differences in relation to various collision metrics. The prevailing opinion suggests that these differences are tied to nuclear structure, particularly the properties of low-lying excited states. A clear link between low-energy nuclear physics and high-energy physics is still lacking. This paper proposes establishing a connection between the two by utilizing thermal density matrices of preheated nuclei, with temperature serving as a parameter to determine which excited states should be considered. A semiclassical flucton method at finite temperatures is also suggested for calculating these thermal density matrices.

We have developed a new probabilistic model to find noisy patterns in sparse binary data by introducing a novel binary latent variable model, inspired by the 'Noisy-OR' concept (Heckerman, 1990). The proposed model can identify hidden structures in noisy data sets, as illustrated by extracting meaningful patterns in recordings from retinal neurons. This model can be widely applied to uncover latent patterns in noisy data, with a particular focus on explaining the spikes of individual neurons in terms of interacting cell groups, known as 'Cell Assemblies' (CAs). The proposed binary latent variable model describes the activity of cell assemblies, with an active assembly decreasing the likelihood of neurons within it to be inactive. We trained our model on simulated spike train data mimicking recorded retinal responses to noise and video stimuli. Our model's performance was thoroughly validated, and we also applied it to real-world spiking responses from retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) during a movie stimulus to uncover the underlying structure.

This study examines a three-dimensional ternary system which is a limiting case of the Nakazawa-Ohta model describing triblock copolymers, incorporating interface energy and a long-range interaction term. Although two-dimensional and three-dimensional binary systems, as well as two-dimensional ternary systems, have been extensively researched, the three-dimensional ternary system remains poorly understood, particularly regarding whether its minimizers consist of a finite number of components. Our paper resolves this uncertainty by demonstrating that the number of components in a minimizer is capped by a quantity that depends solely on the system's total masses and interaction coefficients. The primary challenge lies in the three-dimensional structure hindering the separation of the long-range interaction term from the perimeter term, resulting in the unknown shape of minimizers, even at small masses. This is attributed to the lack of a three-dimensional quantitative isoperimetric inequality with two mass constraints, complicating the construction of competing systems.

A novel approach to image communication has emerged, focusing on conveying meaning for artificial intelligence tasks at the expense of image quality. However, certain applications like autonomous driving demand concurrent consideration of both image quality and AI task performance. To address this, researchers propose a task-oriented communication method that balances both pixel-level and semantic-level distortions under a fixed rate constraint, resulting in a rate-distortion optimization problem. A new metric is introduced to measure semantic distortion based on mutual information between reconstructed images and task labels, enabling analytical solutions for the optimal mapping of source images. By applying variational approximation to this problem, the proposed method can efficiently handle multiple AI tasks. Experimental results demonstrate its superiority over traditional image compression methods and deep learning benchmarks in terms of image quality, AI task performance, and multi-task capabilities.

When a polynomial of degree 3 undergoes Chebyshev's method, the resulting polynomial $C_p$ may have a degree of 4, 6 or 7, depending on the specific cubic polynomial $p$. It has been established that if the cubic polynomial $p$ is either unicritical or non-generic, then the Julia set of $C_p$ is a single connected entity. Conversely, if $p$ is neither unicritical nor generic, then the set of cubic polynomials that result in a connected Julia set for $C_p$ can be parameterized by the multiplier of an extraneous fixed point. For the specific family of such cubic polynomials denoted as $C_\lambda$, where the multiplier of an extraneous fixed point is $\lambda$, we have found that the Julia set of $C_\lambda$ is connected whenever $\lambda$ lies within the range $[-1,1]$.

Epilepsy is a widespread neurological condition affecting individuals across all age groups globally. As an alternative to medications or surgery, Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS) has become a viable treatment option. To optimize DBS planning and ensure standardization, developing an algorithm to automatically pinpoint the Anterior Nucleus of Thalamus (ANT) stimulation site is essential due to its complex nature. This research undertakes an in-depth comparison of different localization methods for ANT-DBS, focusing on a traditional registration technique and deep learning-based methods such as heatmap matching and DSNT. Our experimental findings demonstrate that deep learning-based methods can achieve comparable accuracy to human variability and are significantly faster than conventional approaches.

In a coupled system of two fundamental-frequency and second-harmonic fields with quadratic terms, we investigate the dynamics of 2D truncated Airy waves and three-component solitons. This system models optical media and atomic-molecular mixtures in Bose-Einstein condensates. We find that the system sustains stable solitons and truncated-Airy-waves states in the fundamental-frequency components, represented by exact solutions that are more stable than their degenerate counterparts. By systematically simulating the interactions between truncated Airy waves, we observe the fusion of input into a pair of narrow solitons when the waves are bending in opposite directions through the second-harmonic field, contrasting the behavior in the 1D system. The interaction of waves with identical imprinted vorticities creates additional solitons, while waves with opposite vorticities produce small-amplitude "debris." Furthermore, soliton collisions with heavy truncated Airy waves exhibit a range of outcomes, including bounce-back for slowly moving solitons, absorption for fast solitons, and quasi-elastic passage. In soliton-soliton collisions, lower-velocity solitons merge into a single mode, while higher-velocity solitons pass through each other elastically.

When amorphous solids are subjected to mechanical stress, they exhibit plastic behavior and their elastic response can be suppressed by plastic events that occur within the solid. This suppression, or "screening," can be triggered by quadrupolar plastic events that are densely packed and interact with each other in a way that mimics the behavior of dipole sources. This effect has been studied in amorphous granular systems and has now been extended to classical glass formers, which are composed of point particles interacting through binary forces, such as inverse power law forces and Lennard-Jones interactions. Our research shows that in both of these systems, the elastic response can be significantly suppressed, as predicted by a new theoretical framework. This suppression can be quantified using a novel measure that is dependent on the amount of energy lost to plastic behavior.

A novel model for processing information with read-once linear decision trees involves using $\mathbb{F}_2$ linear forms to query information, with each path containing linearly independent queries. Two variations of this model are explored - weakly and strongly read-once models - which encompass traditional read-once decision trees and parity decision trees. Key findings include the following.

  -  The average-case difficulty of certain functions is examined. A new class of functions called directional affine extractors is defined and proven to be challenging on average for the strongly read-once model. A specific construction of these functions with favorable properties is presented. This builds upon previous research by Cohen and Shinkar (ITCS'16) on parity decision trees. Due to the importance of these functions, the new class is expected to have applications beyond the context of this study.
  -  The relationship between proof complexity and the resolution system $\text{Res}[\oplus]$ is investigated. A connection is established between refutations in $\text{Res}[\oplus]$ and the ability of linear decision trees to solve search problems. Conversely, a weakly read-once linear decision tree can be transformed into a $\text{Res}[\oplus]$ refutation with a minimal increase in computational complexity.

We introduce a two-stage systematic approach for developing efficient approximation algorithms using Lyapunov functions. In the initial phase, Lyapunov functions are utilized to yield a continuous-time approximation algorithm with a guaranteed approximation ratio. The second stage then transforms this algorithm into a discrete-time format, maintaining a similar approximation ratio along with provable computational efficiency. Our method's key advantage lies in the ability to work with the general form of Lyapunov functions, whose specifics are only determined at the end of the first stage through optimization of the continuous-time algorithm's approximation ratio. The use of Lyapunov functions offers several benefits, including the integration of numerous existing algorithms, a framework for designing and analyzing new algorithms, and potential improvements to existing algorithms. Our method is demonstrated through its application to submodular maximization problems.

A collection of sets is considered intersecting when any two sets within it share a common element.  A collection of sets \(\mathcal{C}\) possesses the Helly property if every subset of intersecting sets also shares a common element.  A graph exhibits Helly properties if the sets of its maximal complete subgraphs meet this criterion.  We demonstrate that for a \(k\)-regular graph with \(n\) vertices, where \(n\) surpasses the threshold of \(3k + \sqrt{2k^{2} - k}\), its complement \(\bar{G}\) fails to exhibit the Helly property.  Furthermore, we investigate the relationships between the Helly property and the convergence of the clique graph operator in the context of the complement of \(k\)-regular graphs, focusing on instances where \(k\) takes on small values.

Revisiting a previously noted phenomenon, we examine why the Noether current related to local scale symmetry, or equivalently, Weyl symmetry, always equals zero. Utilizing the second Noether theorem, we demonstrate that the Noether current associated with Weyl symmetry is typically zero within four-dimensional Riemannian geometry-based Weyl-invariant gravitational theories. The underlying reason for this finding is the non-dynamical nature of the Weyl transformation, specifically its lack of derivative terms for the transformation parameter, unlike traditional gauge transformations. We further apply this discovery to a quantum model of Weyl-invariant gravity, deriving currents associated with the $IOSp(10|10)$ supersymmetry, also known as chiral symmetry.

For self-driving vehicles, precise 3D object detection is crucial, and point cloud-based methods have gained popularity due to their accurate depth measurements. A large and diverse dataset like NuTonomy's nuScenes surpasses commonly used datasets like KITTI, but it has a severe class imbalance issue. A proposed solution, the Class-balanced Grouping and Sampling method, aims to rectify this imbalance through augmentation and sampling strategies. Nevertheless, the model's localization accuracy is compromised by the downscaled feature maps, leading to the loss of spatial information. To address this, an auxiliary network is designed to leverage the structural information of 3D point clouds, thereby enhancing the model's localization accuracy. This auxiliary network is jointly optimized using two point-level supervision methods, and it doesn't add any extra computational load during inference since it can be detached at test time.

The Aegis Combat System is a command and control implementation in our application, consisting of missile guidance and tracking as key elements. To investigate these components in detail, we will design a simplified model of the system. In this model, a small-scale autonomous car will mimic the movement of a small-scale remote-controlled car. The system will comprise the controller and two miniature vehicles. This simplified representation will enable the team to illustrate real-world command and control concepts, such as command, communication, and data integration, as shown in Figure 1, an image of the Aegis Combat System.

Fuzzy-Trace Theory and similar decision-making models propose that people primarily use the key takeaway or overall essence of text when making decisions. This study outlines the development process of GisPy, a free, open-source Python tool that calculates the Gist Inference Score in text. Experimental results using texts from news and scientific domains in three benchmark evaluations show that the scores generated by GisPy are highly effective at distinguishing documents with low vs. high gist content. GisPy can be accessed and utilized through a publicly available repository located at: https://github.com/phosseini/GisPy.

In weakly supervised text classification, training a deep neural classifier with pseudo-labels is common but the quality of these labels is vital, yet they inevitably contain errors due to their heuristic nature. Selecting reliable pseudo-labels could significantly enhance performance, so we investigated methods for choosing the right ones. Initially, we explored selecting samples based on the neural classifier's confidence scores corresponding to their pseudo-labels but our experiments showed this approach was ineffective due to poorly calibrated models producing overconfident, yet incorrect, predictions. Recent studies revealed that deep neural models first learn well-labeled samples, followed by those with incorrect labels. Building on this, we introduced a novel pseudo-label selection method called LOPS, which considers the learning order of samples. We theorized that the learning order reflects the likelihood of incorrect annotations, so we proposed selecting the samples that were learned earliest. Through experiments on four real-world datasets, we found that LOPS can greatly enhance the performance of most existing weakly-supervised text classification methods, effectively serving as a performance-enhancing add-on.

The faithfulness of an explanation is crucial for various reasons including trust, 
interpretability, and pinpointing where models go wrong. In this study focused on 
the NLI task, we present Faithfulness-through-Counterfactuals - a new approach 
that first creates a counterfactual hypothesis from the explanation's logical 
components and then checks if the model's prediction aligns with that logical 
understanding. Unlike previous methods, this one doesn't need separate explanation 
data for a verification model. Initially, we verify the effectiveness of automatically 
generating counterfactual hypotheses using the few-shot priming technique. We then 
show that our metric can distinguish between model and human agreement or 
disagreement on novel counterfactual inputs. Furthermore, we conduct a sensitivity 
analysis to confirm that our metric responds to unfaithful explanations.

We explore how guided photons transmit angular momentum to a two-level atom with a specific electric quadrupole transition when positioned near an optical nanofiber. The process by which the guided field's axial orbital torque affects the atom is controlled by the internal-state selection rules for the quadrupole transition and the principle of angular momentum conservation, taking into account the photon's angular momentum as described in Minkowski formulation. The resulting torque is found to be influenced by the photon's angular momentum, the change in the atom's internal state angular momentum, and the quadrupole-transition Rabi frequency. Numerical calculations of the torque were performed for the quadrupole transitions between specific sublevels of a $^{87}$Rb atom, including those between the sublevel $M=2$ of the hyperfine-structure level $5S_{1/2}F=2$ and the sublevels $M'=0$, 1, 2, 3, and 4 of the hyperfine-structure level $4D_{5/2}F'=4$. We discovered that, except in a particular case, the absolute value of the torque for a higher-order mode is larger than that of the fundamental mode, except in a specific case where the higher-order mode's torque is zero.

Our initial research investigates the combination of the isoscalar pseudoscalar meson $\eta$ and the pseudoscalar glueball $G$ within $N_f=2$ QCD at a pion mass of approximately 350 MeV. We have accurately determined the $\eta$ mass as 714.1 MeV, with an uncertainty of 5.4 MeV. Through the Witten-Veneziano relation, this value is consistent with the estimated mass of its $SU(3)$ counterpart, which is approximately 935 MeV. Utilizing a large gauge ensemble and the distillation method to analyze the $\eta-G$ correlators, we have calculated the $\eta-G$ mixing energy and angle, finding values of $|x|=107(14)$ MeV and $|\theta|=3.47(46)^\circ$ respectively. Additionally, we have established that the $\eta$ mass can be accurately derived from correlators of $\eta$ and $\eta_c$, the pseudoscalar charmonium. Our research suggests that $\eta$-glueball mixing is negligible, with the QCD $U_A(1)$ anomaly being responsible for a significant contribution to the $\eta$ mass through topology-induced interaction.

The effectiveness of goal-oriented dialogue systems is not only crucial for achieving user objectives but also depends on how users perceive them as helpful. Unfortunately, there has been limited research into how humans perceive the helpfulness and fairness of these systems. In this study, we investigate using computational metrics to measure the helpfulness of dialogue systems. First, we establish a clear definition of what makes a dialogue response helpful: relevance, coherence, usefulness, and informativeness. We then gather human evaluations of dialogue responses based on this definition and develop a model to automatically assess a response's helpfulness. Furthermore, we propose a method to evaluate the fairness of dialogue systems by analyzing how their helpfulness varies in response to queries from different regions. Our experiments with cutting-edge dialogue systems under three different scenarios have revealed a concerning trend: existing systems tend to be more effective when answering questions about topics from more developed nations than from less developed ones, highlighting potential fairness issues in current goal-oriented dialogue systems.

In recent years, a significant shift has occurred in how learned representations are generated, focusing specifically on point clouds. While these representations have grown increasingly complex, they still often struggle with producing ordered sets of points. To address this issue, we've developed a novel sampling model called Spotlights, which converts a 3D shape into a compact 1D array of depth values by simulating a set of cameras evenly spaced on a sphere. These virtual cameras cast light rays through a small spherical cap, allowing the model to identify potential intersections with the surrounding object. By using this structured approach, we can represent point clouds implicitly as a function of depth. A detailed analysis of the model's geometric structure reveals its effectiveness in point cloud completion tasks, outperforming other methods in terms of accuracy, consistency, and computational efficiency. Moreover, our method achieves superior results in point cloud registration compared to state-of-the-art completion methods when applied to downstream tasks.

Recent studies on language models have exposed a significant risk of data 
privacy due to the memorization of training data during the pre-training phase.
Notably, the risks associated with the fine-tuning phase remain largely 
unexplored. As the "pre-train and fine-tune" method gains popularity, it's crucial 
to understand how various fine-tuning techniques impact the vulnerability to 
privacy threats. This study aims to investigate the susceptibility of 
fine-tuning methods to membership inference and extraction attacks, revealing 
substantial differences in their attack susceptibility. Notably, our results 
indicate that fine-tuning the model head poses the greatest threat to data 
privacy, whereas fine-tuning smaller adapters appears to be less vulnerable.

Recent lightweight fine-tuning methods have been successfully utilized for efficient knowledge transfer by updating only a small number of additional parameters in conjunction with a frozen pre-trained language model. However, the existing literature lacks a comprehensive understanding of whether and how such an approach during fine-tuning affects the pre-training phase. In our study, we demonstrate that considering the final fine-tuning strategy enhances the effectiveness of parameter-efficient fine-tuning. By leveraging optimization-based meta-learning with a customized version of MAML, we adapt the pre-trained model specifically for efficient fine-tuning, achieving improvements of up to 1.7 points in cross-lingual NER fine-tuning. Furthermore, our ablation studies and analyses confirm that the introduced modifications to MAML are essential for obtaining the observed gains.

At the Paul Scherrer Institut's PSI, the High Intensity Proton Accelerator's (HIPA) cyclotron produces a continuous 590 MeV proton beam, yielding 1.42 MW of power. After extraction, the beam is transferred to a 120-meter-long channel to reach two target stations for surface muon production before dissipating energy at the spallation target SINQ. As part of the High Intensity Muon Beamline (HIMB) study, a thicker target will replace the current one to boost muon production. Nevertheless, maintaining the lowest proton beam losses is a crucial challenge for HIMB, which can only be achieved by refining our comprehension of distributed losses along the beamline. To address this, researchers have developed a new strategy that involves linking temperature, beam profile, and current measurements to Monte Carlo simulation tools, thereby correlating experimental values with combined power deposition calculations and primary beam losses.

In 1984, Gauduchon studied an integral involving the square of the norm of the torsion of a $1$-form on a compact Hermitian manifold, which led him to derive an Euler-Lagrange equation for this integral and to find that for 2-dimensional manifolds with vanishing torsion the metrics had to be balanced. This note extends this result to higher dimensions, showing that balanced metrics are critical in all dimensions, and further investigates a more comprehensive integral of the Chern torsion to find instances where critical metrics do not correspond to Kahler manifolds.

We investigate how eccentricity influences the accuracy of gravitational wave parameter estimates for binary neutron star systems. When signals with low eccentricity are injected into the advanced LIGO sensitivity range and we apply a model that assumes circular orbits, we observe biases in the recovered parameters. Specifically, we focus on three intrinsic parameters - the chirp mass, symmetric mass ratio, and tidal deformability. By comparing the Bayesian and Fisher-Cutler-Vallisneri methods, we establish criteria for when the latter approach is valid. Using the Fisher-Cutler-Vallisneri method and a realistic population of binary neutron star sources, we determine the measurement errors and systematic biases for the parameters. Our results show that as eccentricity increases, biases become larger and this growth accelerates. These biases are primarily determined by the level of eccentricity and only weakly influenced by the component masses, resulting in a narrow range of possible values in the eccentricity-bias plane. To illustrate our findings, we provide multiple examples of posterior distributions, including a demonstration of how ignoring eccentricity can lead to incorrect conclusions about the neutron star equation of state.

This paper introduces a semi-supervised learning approach called Generative Self-Training for visually grounded dialog, which exploits unlabeled web images to increase training data. The method first collects relevant images using out-of-distribution detection and generates dialogues related to them using multimodal text generation. It then trains a dialog agent on the synthetically created and original VisDial data, significantly scaling the training data up from 1.2 million to 12.9 million questions and answers. To enhance the reliability of the generated dialogues, we also propose a data selection method based on perplexity and a multimodal consistency regularization technique. Evaluation results on VisDial v1.0 and v0.9 datasets demonstrate that our approach achieves the current best performance on both datasets and shows notable improvements in low-data scenarios with a gain of up to 9.35 absolute points in NDCG.

To combat errors in difficult-to-access qubits, researchers utilize'spectator qubits,' highly sensitive to noise, which are frequently measured and occasionally used to correct the data qubits. A novel, Bayesian approach involving complex linear transformations was devised to develop an adaptive measurement strategy for mitigating dephasing caused by random telegraph noise, demonstrating that using spectator qubits can be highly effective in certain circumstances.

Text generation systems often struggle with unfaithfulness. For Data-to-Text (D2T) systems, the accuracy of the generated text is essential for real-world use. We developed R2D2, a training framework that tackles D2T unfaithfulness by training a model to generate and evaluate text, with tasks to identify incorrect information and learning from unlikely outcomes. To support training, we offer two methods to generate unreliable text. We also believe that a primary reason for D2T inaccuracies is the system's inability to identify entities, so we added new metrics based on named entity recognition to measure the accuracy of D2T output. Our results demonstrate that R2D2 systems can effectively address unfaithfulness and set new standards for performance on FeTaQA, LogicNLG, and ToTTo, with considerable improvements.

The primary objective of this thesis is to investigate potential attack pathways targeting the Iota network's 2.0 protocol version through in-depth analysis. In this work, we examine existing attack vectors in Distributed Ledger Technologies, evaluate their relevance to the Iota 2.0 protocol, and identify a particular attack exploiting honest users' ability to write to the ledger within a network of nodes using full node software.

The development of effective massively multilingual image captioning systems has been hindered by a scarcity of high-quality evaluation datasets. To address this issue, we introduce the Crossmodal-3600 dataset (XM3600), which comprises a geographically diverse collection of 3600 images annotated with human-translated captions in 36 languages. These images were carefully chosen from around the world to reflect the regions where the 36 languages are spoken. Our captions exhibit consistent style across languages while minimizing translation-based artifacts. When utilizing the XM3600 dataset as a benchmark for evaluating massively multilingual image captioning models, we achieve more accurate correlation with human assessments than previously obtained with automatic metrics.

We present FLEURS, a benchmark that evaluates the universality of speech representations through few-shot learning in 102 languages. Constructed upon the machine translation FLoRes-101 benchmark, this parallel speech dataset contains around 12 hours of speech guidance per language. FLEURS encompasses various speech applications such as Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), Speech Language Identification, Translation, and Retrieval. Our study introduces baselines for these tasks leveraging multilingual pre-trained models like mSLAM, aiming to facilitate speech technology in multiple languages and stimulate low-resource speech comprehension research.

We derive the conditions for the existence, uniqueness, and the bounds on the regularity of the given Cauchy problem involving pseudo-differential operators with time-dependent symbols in weighted L_p-spaces. The pseudo-differential operator in question involves a Fourier transform and the weighted L_p-spaces are based on the Muckenhoupt weights. Specifically, we determine the conditions on the symbol, which are related to its smoothness, to ensure that the equation is well-posed. Moreover, we establish two regularity estimates for any solution to the equation, which relate the L_p-norms of the solution and the forcing term with respect to time and space. The regularity estimates are expressed in terms of the operator order, the weights, and the parameters of the equation, which are constrained to satisfy certain conditions to ensure the validity of the estimates.

Event extraction's progress is hindered by a scarcity of data and an imbalance in it. To address this challenge, we've developed a self-training with gradient guidance (STGG) framework, which comprises two components. First, a base event extraction model is trained using existing annotations, then it's applied to large-scale unlabeled corpora to predict new event mentions. Next, a scoring model evaluates each predicted event trigger and argument in the context of their path within an Abstract Meaning Representation graph. This evaluation generates a probability score reflecting the correctness of the prediction. The new predictions and their associated scores are used to refine the base model, leveraging the scores as pseudo-labels that guide the magnitude and direction of its gradients. Our experiments across ACE05-E, ACE05-E+, and ERE-EN datasets show that STGG enhances event extraction performance by up to 1.9 F-score over the base model. Furthermore, we've demonstrated that STGG is a versatile framework, capable of boosting various base event extraction models with minimal dependence on high-quality annotations for Abstract Meaning Representation graphs.

The cartoon domain has gained significant attention in recent times, with past research attempting to achieve high-quality portrait stylization, albeit with difficulties in addressing critical constraints, including a high need for extensive training images and limited support for abstract cartoon faces. Recent advancements using layer swapping methods have partially addressed these challenges but still present narrow use cases due to inheriting residual issues. This paper introduces a novel approach called Cross-domain Style mixing, which involves combining two distinct latent codes to achieve effective face stylization across multiple cartoon characters at various levels of abstraction, utilizing only a single generator and minimal training images.

We're examining the reliability of multilingual question-answering systems that draw upon multiple languages to derive the best possible answers. Our hypothesis suggests that such systems are susceptible to inconsistent information when dealing with documents written in different languages due to variations in topic coverage. To delve deeper into this issue, we investigate the behavior of these systems with a focus on retrieval bias by analyzing the disparities in passages retrieved by various models for the same question in different languages on TyDi QA and XOR-TyDi QA datasets. We speculate that differences in document content across languages may stem from cultural discrepancies or societal biases.

We introduce a pioneering resampling-based approach to develop a highly accurate statistical test for any set of hypotheses in high-dimensional linear regression models. This technique can be seamlessly integrated into existing multiple testing procedures to provide reliable statements about influential predictor variables. By utilizing permutation test statistics and data splitting, along with a variable selection technique, we generate test statistics for individual hypotheses and aggregate these to formulate a subset-level test. Our novel procedure offers remarkable versatility, enabling the use of various selection techniques and combining functions. We provide implementations for both an exact and an approximate version of the method, which is optimized for faster computation and scalability to large datasets. To demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, we present results from simulated data and an analysis of real-world gene expression data.

Current machine translation models still face difficulties with more complex inputs such as noisy data and less common phrases. Researchers have tackled this robustness problem by focusing on specific types of noise and adjusting the models to handle them more effectively. One area that has received relatively little attention involves minor, non-typos variations in language that maintain the original meaning. We identify this category as Natural Asemantic Variation (NAV) and investigate how machine translation models perform under its influence. Our findings show that existing machine translation models are not equipped to handle NAV, but we propose methods for improving their performance using human-generated variations. Additionally, we find that enhancing models to handle NAV for one language can also benefit models for other languages, and synthetic variations can offer some benefits, though they fall short of the advantages provided by organic NAV data.

Key mathematical techniques, including discrete integration and gradient descent optimization, require linear algebra and are typically applied to state vectors in Euclidean spaces as described in literature. However, to utilize these methods with state vectors representing rotations and rigid body motions, a different approach is necessary. This article explores the properties and representations of SO(3) and SE(3) Lie groups, providing a detailed analysis of their tangent spaces, perturbations, and Jacobians in order to adapt common calculus methods for non-Euclidean state vectors.

We examine the eigenbundle (localization bundle) of specific Hilbert modules over symmetric bounded domains of rank $r$, leading to complex-analytic fibre spaces that have a stratified structure of length $r+1.$ The fibers are described within the context of K\"ahler geometry as sections of line bundles over flag manifolds, and the metric embedding is found by taking derivatives of reproducing kernel functions. Notable instances include the determinantal ideals specified by vanishing conditions on the various strata of this stratification.

Large pre-trained language models are known for producing coherent text but have difficulty producing it in response to specific requirements. This work investigates controlled sampling from these models: generating text that adheres to user-specified criteria without compromising its coherence and the model's performance on subsequent tasks. We present MuCoLa, a sampling method that integrates a model's likelihood with custom (differentiable) constraints within a unified scoring function and then generates outputs in a non-sequential manner. It starts with an entire sequence of random values and follows a chain reaction driven by Langevin Dynamics using the gradients of the scoring function. We test MuCoLa's effectiveness in text generation under soft and hard constraints, as well as their combinations, and achieve substantial gains over comparable baselines in reducing toxicity, managing sentiment, and producing keyword-driven content.

Similar to other cybersecurity domains, machine learning has become a promising solution for detecting Android malware. Although numerous studies have proposed various algorithms and feature sets, achieving impressive detection rates, a lack of standardization in evaluation methods makes it challenging to compare results. This paper conducts an analysis of 10 notable studies on Android malware detection using a unified evaluation framework. By investigating the effects of five critical factors on machine learning models - duplicated samples, label attribution, class imbalance, evasion techniques, and app evolution - we found that the optimistic results of ML-based detectors are likely a result of suboptimal evaluation conditions. Consequently, it is essential to create realistic experimental scenarios, considering these factors, to develop more effective ML-based solutions for Android malware detection.

Modern natural language processing (NLP) systems heavily rely on Large Language Models, which deliver outstanding performance and stability across a wide range of tasks and fields. However, their processing demands can make using them costly and challenging. Researchers have been investigating methods such as pruning, quantization, and knowledge distillation to reduce the computational load of these models. This study examines how models pruned through Gradual Unstructured Magnitude Pruning can adapt to new domains and tasks. Experimental results reveal that models pruned early during the training process using general masked language models can effectively transition to new domains and tasks without extensive fine-tuning or specialized techniques. Moreover, our sparse model, Sparse*BERT, demonstrates that it can be transformed into a specialized model, such as SparseBioBERT, by retraining it on specific biomedical data.
