This adaptation allows SparseBioBERT to achieve comparable quality to BioBERT while significantly reducing its parameter count to just 10%.

Cellular extensions at the forefront of a cell are crucial for detecting environmental signals and facilitating cell movement and expansion. Recent research suggests that these protrusions envelop extracellular fibers. The underlying mechanisms of this enveloping process are not yet fully understood. This study integrates theoretical analysis and experimental findings to investigate how cell protrusions coil around fibers with different shapes and geometries. A proposed model explains how curved membrane proteins contribute to protrusion growth and identifies the factors influencing protrusion orientation, including bending and adhesive energies. The model predicts that cells coil their leading-edge around circular fibers, but this behavior is disrupted in fibers with flat cross-sections. These predictions were validated through high-resolution imaging of cells coiling around suspended fibers. This research provides a comprehensive theoretical framework that is supported by experimental evidence and offers insights into the behavior of cellular protrusions on fibers with varying diameters.

Deep learning models face challenges when trained on cardiac magnetic resonance imaging due to the limited amount of expert-annotated data and the complex nature of this data source. Recently, self-supervised contrastive learning (SSCL) has shown promising results in several medical imaging tasks. Nevertheless, it remains uncertain whether SSCL representations primarily capture the organ of interest or adjacent, non-relevant tissue. This research investigates how to effectively incorporate prior knowledge of anatomy into the SSCL training process, focusing on using segmentation networks to pinpoint the heart within CMR images and subsequent pretraining in multiple diagnostic tasks. The results show that incorporating anatomical knowledge can significantly enhance the accuracy of downstream diagnostic tasks. Additionally, pretraining SSCL with in-domain data generally improves downstream performance and yields human-like attention maps, compared to end-to-end training and networks pre-trained on ImageNet. Surprisingly, however, integrating anatomical knowledge into the pretraining process does not yield significant benefits.

This research investigated the influence of repulsive nucleon-nucleon forces resulting from the Pauli exclusion principle on the half-lives of heavy, even-even nuclei, specifically those with atomic numbers between 84 and 92. We incorporated the Pauli exclusion principle into our analysis by adjusting nucleon-nucleon interactions according to the Bohr-Sommerfeld quantization rule and by modifying the double-folding method with a kinetic energy term based on the overlap between alpha and daughter nuclei. Results showed that when we accounted for kinetic energy using the extended Thomas-Fermi approach, our calculations of alpha decay half-lives matched experimental data more accurately than when we didn't.

The exotic nuclear properties in highly neutron-rich isotopes of calcium, nickel, zirconium, and tin have been studied using a complex theoretical approach that combines the Skyrme Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov theory with the Green's function method. The results accurately predict the measured energy costs for removing two and one neutrons from these isotopes. Notably, the theoretical predictions of the neutron drip line, which marks the boundary beyond which neutrons can no longer be bound, differ significantly depending on whether two-neutron or one-neutron separation energies are used. The study found that the pairing energies, which arise from the attractive interaction between neutrons in the nucleus, are weaker in odd-numbered nuclei due to the absence of a neutron paired with an unpaired neutron. Theoretical investigations of the neutron distribution and density of the neutron-rich isotopes revealed the presence of halo structures, characterized by unusually large radii and diffuse density distributions. These effects are largely due to the presence of neutrons in low-lying orbitals with low angular momenta, which extend the nuclear density and increase the radii. The number of neutrons in these extended orbitals shows a similar behavior to the pairing energies, further highlighting the importance of pairing correlations in the formation of halo structures in these neutron-rich isotopes.

DeGroot-style opinion formation operates under the assumption of sustained interactions within a social network, making it unsuitable for agents that temporarily interact with its members. Many real-world organisations and individuals fit this profile. As an example, a company attempting to influence product purchases is limited by time constraints. We've developed a DeGroot model extension that accounts for temporary interactions between external and permanent agents, enabling us to explore optimal methods for an external agent's influence in opinion formation through analysis and simulation.

As complex networked control systems expand in scale, the need to assess their ability to withstand disruptions becomes increasingly crucial. A new wave of research has emerged, using graph theory to redefine traditional system and control principles. This paper provides an in-depth examination of graph-based techniques for evaluating the robustness of networked control systems. It delves into various decentralized algorithms operating within these systems, examining their vulnerability to malicious actions and analyzing the structural properties of their underlying networks. The paper also presents methods to measure the impact of attacks, reinterprets concepts of robustness from a graph-theoretic perspective, and explores additional challenges in networked control system security that rely on graph theory for analysis. Finally, it introduces potential areas for future research in this field.

This presentation delves into the microscopic composition of the non-trivial vacuum fields in QCD, the fundamental building blocks of matter. Employing advanced visualization tools, we investigate the intricacies of centre vortices within these ground-state fields as derived from lattice QCD. Our primary goal is to unravel how dynamical fermions embedded in the QCD vacuum reshape the centre-vortex framework. Notably, the influence of dynamical fermions is substantial and offers novel perspectives on the pivotal role of centre vortices in mediating both confinement and dynamical chiral symmetry breaking within QCD.

When ions are densely packed, the impact of their physical hindrance to one another becomes pronounced, prompting the need to modify the conventional Poisson-Boltzmann equation, which doesn't account for such steric effects.  To address this issue, we investigate the asymptotic behavior of the steady-state Poisson-Nernst-Planck equations that incorporate steric effects, and transform these equations into a Poisson-Boltzmann equation that includes the effects of ion and solvent size.  This new equation features a parameter and positive constants that depend on the size of the ions and solvent molecules.  The new equation's nonlinear term is influenced by the Lambert W function, representing the solvent concentration.  When the parameter goes to zero, the new equation simplifies to the conventional Poisson-Boltzmann equation, but as it increases, a larger parameter value amplifies the repulsive forces between ions and solvent molecules.  This motivates us to examine the asymptotic behavior of the new equation as the parameter goes to infinity under certain boundary conditions, and we prove both theoretically and numerically that it converges to a unique solution of a modified Poisson-Boltzmann equation as the parameter tends to infinity.  Our findings indicate that the new equation's limiting form is a type of modified Poisson-Boltzmann equation, similar to those studied in various earlier works, and can thus be seen as a generalized model of these equations.

Recent advancements in multi-agent reinforcement learning heavily rely on deep neural networks, posing a significant interpretability challenge. Conversely, research into interpretable reinforcement learning has successfully developed methods to derive more understandable decision tree-based policies from neural networks in single-agent settings. To address the existing gap, we introduce a series of algorithms designed to extract interpretable decision tree policies from neural networks trained for multi-agent reinforcement learning. Building on a recent method, IVIPER adapts a single-agent interpretable RL approach to the multi-agent environment. Our results show IVIPER generates high-quality decision tree policies for individual agents. To more effectively model agent interactions, we propose MAVIPER, a centralized training algorithm that jointly develops the decision trees of all agents by predicting their collective behavior. This process utilizes resampling to focus on states critical for interagent interactions. Our evaluation demonstrates that both algorithms outperform baseline results, with MAVIPER-trained agents achieving more synchronized performance in multi-agent particle-world environments compared to IVIPER-trained agents.

The reasoning processes of neural language models are notoriously difficult to interpret.  Recent research has made significant progress in automatically generating machine rationales of their behavior, but the focus has been primarily on developing these rationales rather than using them to improve model performance. A method known as explanation regularization (ER) attempts to enhance neural language model generalization by aligning their machine rationales with human rationales.  However, existing research has largely focused on the models' in-distribution generalization capabilities, with little exploration of their performance in out-of-distribution settings. Furthermore, it remains unclear how ER model performance is impacted by the selection of ER criteria or the number and choice of training instances with human rationales. In response, we have devised ER-TEST, an evaluation framework that assesses ER models' out-of-distribution generalization across three distinct dimensions: unseen datasets, contrast sets, and functional tests. Using ER-TEST, we have investigated three crucial questions: (A) Which ER criteria are most effective for a given out-of-distribution scenario? (B) How does ER model performance change based on the number and selection of training instances with human rationales? (C) Is ER effective even with distantly-supervised human rationales? ER-TEST enables a comprehensive analysis of these questions by considering a diverse range of tasks and datasets. Our research demonstrates that ER has little impact on in-distribution performance, but can yield substantial gains in out-of-distribution performance across various scenarios. Additionally, we have found that the most effective ER criteria depend on the specific task, and that ER can still enhance out-of-distribution performance even with limited or distantly-supervised human rationales.

One of the significant obstacles in reinforcement learning is creating clear and verifiable task definitions. To overcome this challenge, researchers employ a method of outlining tasks through reward machines, which are essentially finite state machines that encapsulate the task to be accomplished. We introduce skill machines, a novel representation that can be directly learned from reward machines, thereby encoding the solution to these tasks. Our framework involves an agent first developing a set of foundational skills in the absence of rewards, and then combining these skills with the learned skill machine to create complex behaviors that conform to any regular language, such as those expressed in linear temporal logics. This enables the agent to seamlessly translate intricate logical task specifications into near-optimal behaviors without requiring any additional learning. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in both a tabular and high-dimensional video game environment, where the agent is faced with numerous complex, long-duration tasks. Our findings indicate that the agent is capable of fulfilling very complex task specifications while achieving near-optimal performance with no further learning required. Furthermore, we show that the performance of skill machines can be enhanced with standard offline reinforcement learning algorithms when optimal behaviors are the primary objective.

Our investigation focuses on the concentration phenomenon for discrete-time stochastic systems that operate within an infinite-dimensional state space. To achieve exponential concentration inequalities, we've established a novel approach grounded in a purely functional analytical framework. Moreover, we've demonstrated that the presence of an exponential-type Lyapunov function not only confers stability in these systems but also yields exponential concentration inequalities when sampling from their stationary distribution via the transport-entropy inequality. These findings hold substantial implications for reinforcement learning and control applications, particularly in obtaining exponential concentration inequalities for unbounded observables without assuming reversibility or precise knowledge of the system, which are typical requirements in statistical mechanics and Markov diffusion processes.

In the realm of circuitry, three fundamental elements are widely recognized: the capacitor, resistor, and inductor. However, Professor Leon Chua proposed the concept of a fourth fundamental element, known as the memristor, which establishes a connection between flux and charge due to symmetrical reasoning in 1971. A physical realization model for the memristor was later published by HP Labs in 2008. The proposed model and its applications are highlighted in this report, emphasizing advantages like variable resistance, adaptability, and no leakage current, along with compatibility with CMOS technology. Different models of the memristor have been developed, each exhibiting distinct characteristics depending on the intended application. As a result, memristor devices are applicable in memory, logic, and neuromorphic systems. A computer model of the memristor would serve as a valuable tool for simulating circuit behavior, facilitating the development of its potential applications as a passive circuit element. This paper presents the simulation results of various VerilogA memristor models under sinusoidal inputs, employing different window functions to verify the accuracy of the models. Additionally, the circuit analysis of these memristor models is conducted.

In Federated Learning, preserving user data privacy is of utmost importance. Although Vision Transformers have been found to be vulnerable to certain attacks, they do train more efficiently with the learned spatial features of position embeddings. However, this efficiency comes at the cost of heightened position sensitivity, putting user data at risk. To counter this risk, enhancing the position-insensitive nature of Vision Transformer models has emerged as a promising approach. Nevertheless, simply removing the position embeddings would not only compromise model performance but also exacerbate the risk to user data. To resolve this dilemma, a novel Masked Jigsaw Puzzle technique has been devised to disrupt the flow of sensitive data. By seamlessly integrating into existing Vision Transformer models, this technique not only improves their performance on large datasets but also significantly enhances their ability to safeguard data privacy against typical attacks.

Existing research on Entity Linking typically assumes a comprehensive reference knowledge base, allowing for complete mention linking, but in reality, this assumption rarely holds as knowledge bases are often incomplete and novel concepts emerge frequently. To address this, this paper established the Unknown Entity Discovery and Indexing (EDIN) benchmark, which integrates novel entities lacking descriptions in the knowledge base and annotated mentions into an existing entity linking framework. By comparing EDIN with zero-shot entity linking, it sheds light on the additional complexities involved. Based on dense-retrieval based entity linking, this paper introduces a comprehensive EDIN pipeline that discovers, clusters, and indexes unknown entity mentions within their context. Experiment results demonstrate that indexing unified entity embeddings derived from multiple mentions yields better performance than indexing mentions individually.

Recent advancements in neural attention models have improved performance on numerous natural language processing tasks. Nevertheless, the quadratic memory complexity of the self-attention module poses a limitation in long text summarization applications. Instead of developing more efficient attention modules, we investigate whether restricted context models can achieve competitive results compared to memory-efficient models that consider global contexts. Our approach splits input into localized segments during both encoding and decoding processes, with individual pages serving as the input unit. We tested our model on various locality principles, from fine-grained sentence-level to coarse-grained document-level. Experimental findings indicate that our locality-aware model outperforms strong baselines employing efficient attention modules, while our analysis provides deeper insights into our modeling strategy.

Recent advancements in Large Language Models (LMs) have led to impressive state-of-the-art results on various Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks. However, the continuous need for improved performance can make it impractical to solely rely on increasing the complexity and size of LMs, considering factors such as high development costs, long training times, and significant environmental impact. An alternative strategy involves leveraging human expertise to rephrase challenging tasks in ways that play to the strengths of LMs, effectively making it easier for them to provide accurate answers. This approach involves humans breaking down complex questions into simpler ones that can be more easily resolved by models. Our research demonstrates that this strategy can lead to substantial performance gains - a 24% increase for GPT3 and a 29% increase for RoBERTa-SQuAD when paired with a symbolic calculator - across a diverse range of datasets involving various reasoning tasks. Our findings suggest that human-in-the-loop question decomposition offers a promising means to augment traditional approaches to developing LMs, thereby opening up new avenues for human involvement in NLP research. The underlying code and data can be accessed at https://github.com/Pruthvi98/QuestionDecomposition.

Surveys serve as vital evidence in shaping policies, making informed decisions, and understanding social dynamics. Nevertheless, conducting comprehensive surveys to yield subpopulation-specific data is resource-intensive and time-consuming. A novel method, Multilevel Regression and Poststratification (MRP), offers a viable solution to derive reliable subpopulation estimates from existing surveys without the need for substantial data. Graphic representations have been extensively utilized to convey and assess MRP estimates; however, there has been a dearth of research on the most effective visualization approaches in this context. This study conducts a systematic literature review to examine the existing practice of MRP visualization and applies MRP to analyze the U.S. 2016 presidential election, leveraging the Cooperative Congressional Election Study (CCES) data to demonstrate the implications of current visualization practices and propose improvements. Our findings indicate that uncertainty is often overlooked in existing visualizations, which is crucial for informed survey-based inferences. Furthermore, we discovered that choropleth maps are predominantly used, yet they only convey point estimates and may obscure valuable information. By employing diverse visualization methods, we showcase the benefits of incorporating uncertainty into visualizations and illustrate how it can highlight the impact of model specifications on estimation outcomes. Additionally, this study presents a strategic approach to visualizing MRP models, taking into account the bias-variance trade-off during evaluation.

As technology shrinks, using parallel processors in hazardous environments like space has raised concerns about runtime errors caused by radiation, also affecting system design. This research proposes an architectural approach to runtime-configurable error tolerance at the core level, incorporating an innovative core redundancy grouping technique called On-Demand Redundancy Grouping (ODRG) into a six-core open-source RISC-V processor cluster. The ODRG scheme enables the cluster to switch between two fault-tolerant modes or high-performance individual core modes, with minimal runtime switching overhead. The ODRG unit requires only a small area addition, comparable to a commercial state-of-the-art solution but with faster fault recovery and negligible timing increase. Moreover, unlike other methods, ODRG optimizes performance by repurposing redundant cores for independent computations, achieving significant speedups in specific applications.

Measuring the similarity between terms, text data, and concepts is a crucial aspect in various applications that handle textual information, including knowledge acquisition, recommendation systems, and natural language processing. In recent years, many structured knowledge bases, known as ontologies, have been developed for information systems and used to represent knowledge in a more organized manner. Building on these advancements, researchers have created multiple methods to calculate semantic similarity based on ontologies, which can be tailored to specific contexts by incorporating additional similarity measurement techniques. This study proposes and explores an approach to calculating semantic similarity based on ontologies in the context of a recommendation system.

For tasks like entity classification and dialogue emotion classification, which are instances of set generation in NLP, traditional Seq2Seq models treat a set as a sequence, overlooking its inherent order-invariance and cardinality properties. We developed an innovative method for efficiently sampling informative orders from the vast set of possible label orders. Our novel approach combines modeling set cardinality and output by prepending the set size and utilizing autoregressive factorization, making it a model-independent data augmentation technique that imbues any Seq2Seq model with the signals of order-invariance and cardinality. When trained on data augmented with our technique without requiring additional annotations, our method yields an average relative improvement of 20% across BART, T5, and GPT-3 models on four benchmark datasets. The SETAUG code is available at https://setgen.structgen.com.

Denoising diffusion probabilistic models have achieved notable success in various generation tasks, however they often require a significant number of iterative denoising steps to produce high-quality samples, which results in low inference efficiency. To address this limitation, a novel acceleration strategy called Early-Stopped DDPM is proposed, which involves halting the diffusion process at an early stage and initiating the reverse denoising process from a non-Gaussian distribution. Furthermore, by incorporating a powerful pre-trained generative model, the sampling process from the target distribution can be efficiently accelerated. As a result, the number of required denoising steps is substantially reduced, and the sample quality significantly improved, surpassing both the vanilla DDPM and the adopted pre-trained model. Through extensive experiments on diverse datasets, Early-Stopped DDPM demonstrates a promising acceleration effect and outperforms benchmark methods. Additionally, it possesses several desirable properties, including independence from existing acceleration techniques and the ability to control image generation at both global and local levels.

Recent advancements in hyperspectral image classification have utilized deep neural networks with promising results, but conventional architectures often overlook the inherent properties of these images, particularly the physical noise inherent in the data. Consequently, such models struggle to produce distinct features necessary for optimal classification. To address this, a novel deep learning approach is introduced, which incorporates a noise-sensitive module and denoising framework to enhance hyperspectral image classification. The proposed method first employs a noise model to account for the high variability within classes and substantial overlap between classes in the image. It then develops a noise-sensitive module to capture the inherent noise and follows this with a denoising framework to eliminate the noise from objects. Ultimately, a deep CNN is designed, which incorporates the noise-sensitive module and denoising framework to produce robust features, leading to improved classification performance. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through experiments on two real-world datasets, and the corresponding implementation can be accessed at the specified GitHub repository.

In situations where data-storage qubits are kept isolated with minimal interference, it's possible to mitigate noise by using additional probes that only apply corrections when necessary. For solid-state qubits, we examined dephasing noise stemming from two-state fluctuations modeled as a random telegraph process, alongside a noise probe in the form of a spectator qubit. Assuming projective measurements on this qubit, we created a theoretical framework and assessed different control strategies when noise mitigation is effective. Initially, we explored the Greedy algorithm, which prioritizes maximizing the data qubit's coherence at every step, and found it to be highly effective. We then identified a simplified approximation of its adaptive strategy and built upon it to create a one-parameter family of algorithms using Bayesian maps. In high-noise scenarios, this family reduces the data qubit's decoherence rate in accordance with the square of its noise sensitivity, ultimately leading to the Map-based Optimized Adaptive Algorithm for Asymptotic Regime. This algorithm was shown to outperform the Greedy strategy, particularly in cases of high noise sensitivity, through both analytical and numerical analysis.

A key message, 'nobody is safe until everybody is safe,' highlights the urgent need for a unified global approach in addressing pandemics like COVID-19, which are deeply interconnected. Focusing on the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic, our research investigates the spread of a virus across interconnected communities. We simulated various vaccination scenarios, considering that vaccine effectiveness wanes over time, using a susceptible-vaccinated-infected-recovered model that includes unvaccinated ("Bronze"), moderately vaccinated ("Silver"), and highly vaccinated ("Gold") communities. These communities interact through different types of networks and a linear diffusive coupling for local spreading. Our results indicate that when the non-vaccinated ("Bronze") community interacts with the moderately vaccinated ("Silver") and highly vaccinated ("Gold") communities, it tends to drive up infections in the latter. This shows a negative effect on vaccinated communities caused by non-vaccinated individuals. Furthermore, our analysis of interactions between "Gold", "Silver" and "Bronze" communities within a network reveals that coupling strength and network density are crucial factors. When considering the spread of a virus in Barabasi-Albert networks, we found that "Gold" communities are most successful in keeping their infection rates low, while a small number of "Bronze" communities can still cause a surge in infections in "Silver" and "Gold" communities. However, in dense Erdos-Renyi networks, all communities eventually reach a disease-free state. Conversely, in sparse Watts-Strogatz and Barabasi-Albert networks, this does not occur, but we also observed that if all these networks were connected and vaccinated, they would reach a disease-free state.

We conducted a theoretical investigation on the $D\bar{D}K$ three-body system, applying the fixed center approximation to the Faddeev equations, which accounts for the $D$-$K$, $D$-$\bar{D}$ interactions based on the chiral unitary approach. This study focuses on the $K$ meson scattering off the $D\bar{D}$ system, potentially forming the scalar meson $X(3720)$. Due to the strong $DK$ interaction, which generates the scalar $D^*_{s0}(2317)$ meson, a resonance pattern emerges in the $K$-$(D\bar{D})_{X(3720)}$ scattering amplitude, supporting the existence of a $D\bar{D}K$ bound state. This outcome is consistent with prior theoretical findings suggesting the existence of a new hidden charm $K$ meson, specifically the $K_{c\bar{c}}(4180)$ with quantum numbers $I(J^P) = \frac{1}{2}(0^-)$ and an estimated mass of about $4180$ MeV. Future experimental searches are likely to be motivated by these theoretical predictions.

In a dynamic resource allocation problem with T divisible resources and n fixed agents, the resources are allocated immediately and permanently based on the agents' stochastic utilities drawn from a known distribution. While most existing solutions aim to maximize the total utility of the agents, this may lead to a concentration of resources among select agents, neglecting others' needs. This paper addresses this issue by adopting an egalitarian welfare approach, which seeks to balance efficiency and fairness in resource allocation. We first investigate a fluid-based policy derived from a deterministic approximation and show it achieves a regret of approximately the square root of T compared to the optimal egalitarian allocation when all utilities are known beforehand. We then propose a new policy, Backward Infrequent Re-solving with Thresholding (BIRT), which involves resolving the fluid problem at most log log T times. This policy achieves an O(1) regret against the optimal allocation regardless of the time horizon T and initial welfare, and numerical experiments confirm its performance improvement over various benchmark policies.

As autonomous systems become increasingly sophisticated, their safety implications become more pronounced in unstructured environments. This research develops a safety protocol for mechanical systems that identifies and addresses instability caused by external disruptions. This safety feature operates separately from existing nominal control systems and intervenes when potential instability arises, limiting power transfer accordingly. The safety layer relies on calculating the Largest Lyapunov Exponent (LLE), a measure of dynamic divergence or convergence rates, to rapidly detect and counter potentially hazardous system behaviors. By integrating the LLE with Control Barrier Functions, power constraints can be imposed on systems controlled by jerks. The effectiveness of this architecture is experimentally demonstrated on an Omnidirectional Micro Aerial Vehicle (OMAV), both in free flight and interactive scenarios.

In the classic cake-cutting problem where divisible resources are shared fairly among n agents, this study focuses on an interesting variant in which agents on a graph evaluate their shares relative to their neighbors. Given a graph, the goal is to find a locally envy-free allocation efficiently. A significant contribution of this work is identifying a non-trivial graph structure - two-layer tree graphs - that allows for a query-efficient cake-cutting protocol with at most O(n^3 log(n)) cuts on the cake. For a specific type of two-layer tree graph, this can be done with just O(n^2) queries. A lower bound is established for a different graph structure, showing that at least O(n^2) evaluation queries are required.

Current cybersecurity threat and risk analysis approaches can only partially automate the process, leaving key decisions to the expertise of teams, which are often made through face-to-face workshops where biased judgments may occur due to underrepresentation of certain demographics. As a result, decisions regarding security risk assessment and mitigation are made under uncertainty, potentially leading to unfair allocation of expertise. Given the scarcity of studies focusing on diversity's influence in technical risk analysis, this study aims to investigate the essential factors contributing to diversity in cybersecurity risk analysis through a controlled experiment.

This study addresses the issue of reduced performance in 5G networks due to mobility in massive MIMO systems. A new channel prediction method, utilizing multi-dimensional matrix pencil (MDMP), is presented to estimate path parameters by leveraging the wideband channel's angular and temporal characteristics. The MDMP approach also incorporates a unique path pairing technique, taking advantage of the high-resolution angle estimation property, to pair Doppler and delay effects. Our method is capable of handling the realistic constraint imposed by user movements on path delays, an aspect previously unexplored in existing literature. It is theoretically proven that under time-varying path delays, the prediction error diminishes as the number of base station antennas increases, provided that only two channel samples are known. Moreover, a lower bound on the number of base station antennas required for satisfactory performance is derived. Simulation results based on the 3GPP industrial channel model demonstrate that our proposed MDMP method achieves performance comparable to stationary scenarios, even at user velocities of 120 km/h and large channel state information latency of 16 ms.

Personalizing interactions between humans and virtual agents involves capturing the behavior style of virtual agents. We propose a machine learning approach to create personalized gestures in the style of various speakers by utilizing prosodic features and text data from multiple sources. Our model can transfer speech styles without retraining by leveraging a database containing videos of various speakers. The style of speech influences the expressiveness of communicative behaviors, while speech content is carried by multimodal signals and text. By separating style and content, our model can infer the style embedding of unseen speakers without additional training. The model consists of two key components: a style encoder that generates a speaker embedding from multimodal data and a sequence-to-sequence synthesis network that produces gestures based on input content and speaker style. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our model by generating gestures of unseen speakers and transferring their style variability. The resulting gestures are then converted into 3D poses to create animated expressions, which we evaluate objectively and subjectively against a baseline to validate our approach.

Consider a non-trivial subgroup H of a finite group G with identity element e. We define a specific type of graph, denoted as the generalized non-coprime graph, where vertices represent elements of G excluding the identity, and two elements are connected by an edge under certain conditions related to their orders and subgroup membership. In this study, we investigate various graph properties for this type of graph, focusing on cyclic groups, and determine the necessary and sufficient conditions for the graph to belong to specific categories such as stars, cycles, or bipartite graphs. We also examine how these results generalize to other types of finite groups, including nilpotent and EPPO groups, before discussing connections to other graph concepts like the Gruenberg--Kegel graph.

A sophisticated compartmental model based on nonlinear partial differential equations simulates COVID-19 spread across space and time. Enhancing spatial resolution, adding compartments, and categorizing by medical criteria significantly increases the number of variables to millions. A high-performance parallel solver efficiently handles complex models, combining techniques like domain decomposition and multigrid preconditioning at various levels to ensure scalability. A specific numerical example demonstrates this approach using a five-stage COVID-19 model for Southern Ontario, achieving accurate three-month infection predictions within seven hours for 92 million individuals, using 1,780 processes, and saving substantial computational time.

Researchers Dorigoni, Green, and Wen proposed a precise equation for the combined correlation of four specific operators within $\mathcal{N}=4$ supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory. This work focuses on the large N limit of their discovery. Our analysis finds that the original equation can be reinterpreted as the sum of individual contributions from $(p,q)$-strings. Due to a specific duality, a single underlying function governs these contributions, mirroring the behavior of fundamental strings. Analyzing the large-order behavior of this function's perturbative expansion allows us to uncover non-perturbative corrections at large N, which we relate to D3-brane instantons within its holographically equivalent type IIB string theory. Our findings align with those obtained using a Laplace-difference equation for the combined correlator.

Determining physical conditions in massive star-forming clouds through
observations requires high sensitivity and resolution, particularly in regions of
high-mass star formation. Our goal is to establish how accurately we can
determine the physical conditions within these clouds through observational data.
We focus on the capabilities of the Next Generation VLA (ngVLA) interferometer,
utilizing magnetohydrodynamic simulation data of star-formation and a filamentary
structure resembling an infrared-dark cloud. Synthetic ngVLA observations are
produced for spectral lines and analyzed for column density, gas temperature,
and kinematics. These results are compared to ideal observations and the actual
3D model, with the goal of assessing the capabilities of the ngVLA. At a distance
of 4 kpc, the ngVLA provides 0.01 pc resolution, even in its most compact
configuration, allowing for the mapping of cloud kinematics and structure at
sub-arcsec scales for abundant molecules like HCO+, NH3, and CO isotopomers.
With NH3, column density maps and kinetic temperatures can be accurately
determined across a 15 x 40 arcsec cloud, even without additional single-dish
data. The ngVLA will provide precise data on the small-scale structure and the
physical and chemical state of clouds in high-mass star-forming regions, even
at kiloparsec distances. However, complementary single-dish data are necessary
for estimates of total column density and large-scale kinematics.

To achieve ultra-reliable, low-latency communication with high efficiency and security, a multi-objective optimization problem is developed for downlink communication in a finite blocklength environment with multiple users and potential eavesdroppers. A complex problem arises from conflicting objectives, non-linear factors, and intertwined variables. To overcome these challenges, a two-phase optimization approach is employed. In the first phase, a lower bound on the secrecy rate is established, and local optimal solutions are derived through a generalized eigenvalue problem solved via power iteration. In the second phase, a weighted-sum approach is utilized to minimize error probabilities and leakage rates for given precoders, and KKT conditions are derived accordingly. Simulations confirm the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm.

We calculate the entanglement entropy between two maximally-extended spacetime regions of a static black hole, separated by the event horizon. We begin by examining the Schwarzschild black hole, and subsequently expand the analysis to include charged Reissner-Nordstrom and Schwarzschild-de Sitter black holes with multiple horizons. Additionally, we investigate the static, spherically-symmetric solution in the context of more general F(R) gravity. Entanglement entropy is computed via the replica trick, using an explicit metric representing the replica spacetime for each black hole type. For static, spherically-symmetric black holes, our results for entanglement entropy confirm the Bekenstein-Hawking area law for entropy.

Deep learning networks have achieved impressive results across numerous applications, but they remain susceptible to a severe vulnerability - adversarial attacks. These attacks subtly alter an input image, rendering it almost imperceptible to the human eye, yet significantly affecting the network's classification outcome. This study delves into the effectiveness of the Projected Gradient Descent (PGD) attack and the Adaptive Mask Segmentation Attack (ASMA) on the DeepLabV3 image segmentation model, employing MobileNetV3 and ResNet50 architectures. The findings reveal that PGD consistently achieves the desired segmentation outcome, whereas ASMA's adaptation to a multiclass target is less effective. Nonetheless, the existence of such attacks poses a threat to all deep learning networks in the image classification domain.

This work introduces a real-time, scalable platform that utilizes predictive uncertainty to drive exploration in the context of real-time bidding. The system operates within a high-performance framework that balances speed and efficiency. Our experiments using online A/B testing reveal that incorporating uncertainty-driven exploration into model-based predictions yields significant improvements in model effectiveness and key business metrics.

A significant hurdle in computational biology is to reconcile the need for accurate and comprehensive data with the complexity of mathematical models that accurately answer key biological questions. Despite the development of tools like identifiability analysis and information criterion to bridge this gap, data limitations often hinder the effectiveness of these approaches. Simple, empirical models such as the logistic and Gompertz growth models are generally identifiable through standard measurements. However, to derive insights from complex, unidentifiable models that incorporate crucial biological mechanisms, researchers examine how non-identifiable parameters relate to identifiable parameters in simpler, related models. By introducing an intermediate layer of interpretation between non-identifiable parameters and metrics like goodness-of-fit, this method reveals the quantitative relationships between these parameters and data features. Our approach has been successfully applied to studying multicellular tumour spheroid growth using a hierarchy of mathematical models, where we could predict non-identifiabilities, categorize non-identifiable parameter spaces into identifiable subsets, and gain valuable biological insights from complex, unidentifiable models.

Calculations for the nucleosynthesis of heavy elements rely heavily on the photon strength functions, which can be experimentally constrained by examining the photo-response of atomic nuclei. To this end, our investigation focuses on the photo-response of $^{66}$Zn within the 5.6 MeV to 9.9 MeV energy range. We have separated the "elastic" decay channel that leads back to the ground state and analyzed the contributions of electric and magnetic dipole transitions in this channel. Using a high-intensity, linearly-polarized quasi-monoenergetic photon beam, nuclear resonance fluorescence experiments were conducted on $^{66}$Zn. Our data analysis extracted the full photoabsorption cross sections, disentangling the average contribution of electric and magnetic dipole strengths for the ground-state decay channel. Furthermore, the average branching ratio back to the ground state was determined. Our results show significantly lower cross sections compared to a previous experiment using bremsstrahlung on $^{66}$Zn, suggesting that the statistical-model calculations used to estimate the branching ratio in the earlier study may have been inaccurate.

Object localization using coarse annotations such as image categories is an
intricate problem. Current deep learning techniques, like class activation maps,
overemphasize specific object parts while overlooking the entire object. 
Recent transformer-based methods predominantly focus on background features, 
impeding the identification of complete objects. To address these limitations, 
we propose the token refinement transformer (TRT) mechanism that utilizes 
object-level semantics to accurately localize objects. The TRT model includes 
a novel token priority scoring module (TPSM) to suppress background noise and 
enhance target object detection. Furthermore, the class activation map serves 
as a semantically informed input, constraining the attention map to the target 
object. Our approach outperforms existing methods when using image category 
annotations, as evident from comprehensive experiments on two benchmarks. The 
source code for our method is available on GitHub at 
https://github.com/su-hui-zz/ReAttentionTransformer.

Recent advancements in Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have shown impressive results across multiple domains, yet these networks are susceptible to data noise and adversarial attacks. Developing a robust GNN capable of withstanding these threats is a critical challenge. Existing defense strategies are resource-intensive and lack scalability. This paper presents a general framework for strengthening GNNs, referred to as the Weighted Laplacian Graph Neural Network (RLW-GNN). The method integrates Weighted Graph Laplacian learning with GNN architecture, leveraging the beneficial properties of the Laplacian matrix, feature smoothness, and latent features within a unified optimization framework. This ensures the removal of noisy or adversarial edges while accurately weighting graph connections. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach using the Graph Convolutional Neural Network (GCNN) architecture, but the framework's versatility allows it to be easily adapted to any existing GNN architecture. Simulation results on benchmark datasets validate the proposed method's performance in both accuracy and computational efficiency, with access to the code provided on https://github.com/Bharat-Runwal/RWL-GNN.

To ensure effective and efficient planning in autonomous racing, accurately forecasting the movement of other competitor vehicles is essential.  Despite their expressive capabilities, deep neural networks present a challenge due to their black-box nature, making them less suitable for high-stakes applications such as autonomous driving.  We propose a structured framework for using deep neural networks to predict the movement of opposing racecars, ensuring that the resulting set of possible trajectories remains constrained. This constraint allows for quality guarantees to be provided on the accuracy of the predictions.  Our model outperforms a baseline architecture, an LSTM-based encoder-decoder model, when evaluated on data from realistic simulations.  The proposed approach meets quality guarantees, paving the way for a robust real-world application.  The developed model was successfully implemented in the Indy Autonomous Challenge 2021 on a vehicle from the Technical University of Munich, and the corresponding code has been made publicly available on GitHub.

Galaxies are often divided into two categories based on star formation and structure: star-forming disk galaxies and passive, spherical galaxies. However, a comprehensive analysis of 4574 galaxies in the local universe reveals a more complex situation. By examining the relationship between velocity and velocity dispersion, it was found that galaxies at a given mass do not fit neatly into two categories. In reality, fast-rotating galaxies comprise multiple populations, including dynamically-cold disks and intermediate systems. These disks account for the majority of both mass and number in this group. Furthermore, while star-forming galaxies are mostly composed of disks, passive galaxies display a mix of disk and spherical forms. Notably, passive disks make up nearly 30% of passive galaxies, a higher percentage than slow rotators. This diversity of galaxy types paints a picture of the local universe, dominated by galaxies with disk-like structures, with most of them transitioning to less rotation-supported forms after quenching.

Tractable density models, specifically normalizing flows, have the ability to approximate intricate target distributions, such as those of complex physical systems. Nevertheless, the prevailing training methods for these flows either exhibit mode-seeking behavior, rely on expensive pre-generated samples via MCMC simulations, or make use of loss functions with considerable variance. In an effort to circumvent these challenges, we have developed a novel approach by integrating normalizing flows with annealed importance sampling (AIS). This method minimizes the mass-covering $\alpha$-divergence when $\alpha=2$, effectively reducing the variance of the importance weights. Our technique, the Flow AIS Bootstrap (FAB), leverages AIS to generate samples in areas where the flow underperforms in approximating the target, thereby enabling the detection of new modes. By applying FAB to intricate multimodal targets, we demonstrate the successful approximation of these complex distributions where other methods fail. Furthermore, FAB has achieved the milestone of learning the Boltzmann distribution of the alanine dipeptide molecule using solely the unnormalized target density, without recourse to MCMC simulations. In comparison, FAB outperforms maximum likelihood training on samples generated by Molecular Dynamics simulations while requiring a mere 1/100th of the evaluations. Following reweighting with importance weights, the resulting histograms of dihedral angles exhibit minimal bias, aligning almost perfectly with the ground truth.

Capturing users' diverse behaviors is a crucial component of modern e-commerce, mainly applied in the joint optimization of click-through and conversion rate predictions. Many current approaches neglect two critical aspects of user behavior: (i) contextual influence, where a user's interactions with one item are influenced by their past actions on other items; (ii) variable time scales, indicating that users tend to click frequently but make purchases sporadically. To address this, we introduce the Hierarchical rEcurrent Ranking On the Entire Space (HEROES) framework, which incorporates contextual information to model users' behaviors at multiple scales. By implementing a hierarchical structure, our model includes a lower layer for tracking user engagement and an upper layer for estimating user satisfaction. The proposed architecture can automatically learn suitable time scales for each layer, enabling the model to capture dynamic behavioral patterns. Furthermore, we introduce a novel recurrent unit based on the Hawkes process, allowing the model to encode item features and incorporate the user's previous behaviors as excitation or discouragement. Additionally, HEROES can be combined with survival analysis to create unbiased ranking systems. Our extensive experiments on three large-scale datasets demonstrate HEROES' superiority over existing methods.

The Lightning Network (LN) has seen rapid expansion, and it has become the preferred scaling solution for the Bitcoin blockchain. LN's security relies on its nodes being able to settle balances by confirming transactions on the Bitcoin blockchain within a predetermined timeframe. The LN's inherent time constraint makes it vulnerable to attacks that aim to overload the Bitcoin blockchain, disrupting protocol execution. We examine the LN's susceptibility to "mass exit" attacks carried out by a small group of malicious nodes. These attacks force numerous honest protocol participants to interact with the blockchain. We analyze two types of attacks: (i) a "zombie" attack where nodes become unresponsive to lock funds in channels for longer than allowed by LN's protocol. (ii) a "mass double-spend" attack where nodes submit multiple transactions to steal funds by exploiting expired protocol states, prompting honest nodes to submit invalid transactions. Simulation results show that under realistic congestion conditions and mild assumptions about channel balances, both attacks can be carried out by a small group of nodes. We formulated the problem of finding the worst-case group of malicious nodes as a graph cut problem to support our experimental findings, which are justified by the LN's scale-free network topology.

Our research focuses on discovering new cataclysmic variable stars (CVs) and identifying potential candidates of AR Scorpii-type binary systems. We began by identifying GAIA sources associated with unidentified X-ray sources, and then examined the light curves captured by the Zwicky Transient Facility, Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite, and Lulin One-meter Telescope. From our analysis, eight sources emerged as CV candidates, with six being newly identified. Two additional sources, previously recognized as CVs, received more in-depth investigation. We found two systems displaying eclipses, linked to unidentified XMM-Newton or Swift sources, and one candidate that might be a polar linked to an unidentified ASKA source. Two polar candidates could be situated in the so-called period gap of CV systems, while the other six candidates have orbital periods below this gap. Although we didn't find a suitable candidate for AR Scorpii-type binary systems, our study implies that CV systems emitting X-rays but infrequently producing outbursts may have been overlooked in previous surveys.

Most studies of layered fluid instabilities have made the unrealistic assumption that shear and buoyancy gradients coincide. We investigate how asymmetry impacts the development of shear instabilities by employing both linear theory and direct numerical simulations. The results show that asymmetry leads to instabilities combining characteristics of both Holmboe and Kelvin-Helmholtz instabilities, and a method is developed to identify whether the instabilities resemble either type more closely. Furthermore, asymmetry induces uneven mixing patterns with features from both upturning and erosion flows, and it tends to realign the shear and buoyancy gradients. Notably, in nearly all but the symmetric Kelvin-Helmholtz simulations, we observe a convergence in the distribution of the Richardson number, indicating that asymmetry reduces the dependence on parameters for Kelvin-Helmholtz-driven mixing. The dependence of the turbulent behavior on small-scale aspects of shear and stratification has significant implications for the interpretation of oceanographic data.

Over the past few years, significant progress has been made in unpaired image denoising. Nevertheless, the performance of most methods heavily relies on unrealistic assumptions about noise properties. To overcome this limitation, our approach focuses on a structural perspective of the problem, leading to a more robust solution. Motivated by this idea, we propose an unpaired, self-supervised denoising technique based on spatial degradation and refined regularization, which outperforms existing methods across various datasets and consistently demonstrates reliable results.

A transmembrane integrin protein plays a significant role in cell membrane dynamics by reorganizing the actin network and linking it to the extracellular matrix through complex mechanical processes. Integrin facilitates the formation of specific lipid and protein clusters that are crucial for certain endocytosis mechanisms at specific active membrane regions. To understand this phenomenon, we have developed a simplified mathematical model that accounts for the interaction between integrin's on and off states and the natural movement of the cell membrane. This model enables us to derive a precise equation for membrane deformation and velocity, as well as lipid clustering driven by a single integrin. Our results reveal non-linear patterns in membrane deformation, velocity, and lipid clustering, and we have identified their dependence on the duration of stochastic integrin shuttling and membrane characteristics.

Einstein constraint equations are numerically solved on a range of compact, orientable three-dimensional manifolds that possess complex topological features. Calculations yield simple and more complex solutions for mean curvature, each obtained on a distinct manifold from the Thursten geometrization classes. These constant mean curvature solutions simultaneously satisfy the requirements of the Yamabe problem, effectively transforming geometries to ones with uniform scalar curvature.

Homophily, a principle that connects "similar individuals," is quantified in networks by determining whether a given group structure results in significantly denser subgraphs compared to random group assignments with the same characteristics. This "random coloring model" for network homophily views a vector of subgraph sizes as the outcome of randomly picking a group structure from those with the same characteristics. A network is deemed homophilic at a significance level of alpha if the probability of observing the actual subgraph sizes is lower than alpha, which can also represent the degree of homophily. However, approximating this probability is an NP-hard problem, so we use a multidimensional extension of Cantelli's inequality, known as the homophily index, to provide an upper bound. This index requires knowledge of the covariance matrix of subgraph sizes, which we calculate and find to depend only on the group structure and network degrees. This structure leads to a meaningful and easily computable index for measuring network homophily.

The Fabbri-Russo model generalizes a two-dimensional theory of dilaton gravity with adaptable parameters, denoted as "$n$", representing distinct gravity theories. The Russo-Susskind-Thorlacius model specifically aligns with $n=1$. In the context of the Fabbri-Russo model, this study investigates Page curves and the entanglement island within both eternal and evaporating black holes. The emergence of islands leads to decelerated growth of the entanglement entropy of radiation after the Page time, upholding unitarity principles. For eternal black holes, the fine-grained entropy stabilizes at twice the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy, while for evaporating black holes, this entropy eventually reaches zero. The "$n$" parameter significantly influences the Page curve at initial stages but becomes a negligible factor at late times and large distances. Consequently, Page curve shapes are largely independent of "$n$" in leading order. Furthermore, this research examines the relationship between entanglement islands and firewalls, demonstrating the former's potential superiority in addressing the quantum entanglement-monogamy problem. Lastly, this study briefly explores the gravity/ensemble duality as a potential solution to the state conundrum arising from the island formula.

A common technique used to analyze event sequences with timestamps is the temporal point process (TPP). Previous approaches have mainly focused on the accuracy of TPP models by maximizing the likelihood, but their predictive abilities are unsatisfactory. These models often generate timestamps that significantly differ from true observations. Recent advancements in deep generative models have achieved remarkable results in image generation tasks by producing high-quality samples. Despite this, there is a lack of comprehensive studies exploring the potential of generative models in the context of TPP for event occurrence modeling. In this work, we bridge this gap by developing a unified generative framework called GNTPP to investigate its feasibility and effectiveness in improving predictive performance. Additionally, we revise the attentive models used to measure historical impacts by incorporating an adaptive reweighting term that considers event types and time intervals. Our experimental results demonstrate the improved predictive capability of GNTPP with various generative probabilistic decoders and the benefits of the revised attention mechanism. To the best of our knowledge, this work is the first to integrate generative models into a unified framework and examine their effectiveness in TPP. Our codebase is publicly available at https://github.com/BIRD-TAO/GNTPP and aims to facilitate future research in Neural TPPs.

In vehicular networks, Federated edge learning technology is viewed as a key to mitigate computation burdens and safeguard user confidentiality. The system enables vehicles to upload data to edge servers, which process this data to update local models and return the results, thereby keeping the original data private. Despite this, the limited cache capacity in the edge server and time-varying wireless channels pose significant challenges when selecting the ideal number of vehicles to upload data to maintain a stable cache queue while maximizing learning accuracy. Additionally, the choice of vehicles with diverse resource capabilities affects data volumes and subsequently model accuracy. To address this, a vehicle selection method is proposed that balances learning accuracy and cache queue stability, taking into account the resource statuses of all vehicles within the edge server's coverage. The efficacy of this scheme is evaluated through simulation, demonstrating superior performance over a benchmark.
